questions.prompt: The hash after the filename was copied from the image's download page on cisco.com. What should the engineer do next?
options: Proceed with `boot system`; the computed signature is the router's own valid hash of the file
Run `verify /md5` a second time; the first pass on a large file often reports a false mismatch
Re-enter the command without the hash; the router only needs to compute the value itself
Delete the file and transfer it again; the image in flash does not match the published hash
questions.explanation: `verify /md5 file hash` computes the file's MD5 and compares it with the value you supply. A mismatch means the bytes in flash are not the bytes Cisco published — a truncated or corrupted transfer, or the wrong file. Never point `boot system` at it; copy it again and verify again.

whyWrong.0: A hash that differs from the published one proves the file is wrong, however valid it looks locally.
whyWrong.1: MD5 is deterministic; a second run on an unchanged file gives the same result.
whyWrong.2: Without the hash the router only prints the computed value; you still have to compare it with the published one.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the global configuration commands `ip ftp username backup` and `ip ftp password B4ckup-2026`?
options: They create an FTP server on the router that clients log in to with those credentials
They restrict which local usernames are allowed to run `copy ftp:` from EXEC mode
They supply the credentials `copy ftp:` uses when none are given in the URL
They are required for `copy tftp:` because TFTP shares the FTP credential store
questions.explanation: IOS is an FTP client. When a `copy ftp:` URL contains no `user:password@` part, the router logs in with the stored `ip ftp username` and `ip ftp password`, keeping the password out of the command history.

whyWrong.0: IOS does not run an FTP server; these commands configure the client side.
whyWrong.1: They are credentials sent to the server, not an authorisation list for local users.
whyWrong.3: TFTP has no authentication and ignores these commands entirely.

spec.title: R1 backs up to SRV1
spec.caption: R1 and SRV1 share 10.1.1.0/24 through SW1.

questions.prompt: R1 runs `copy running-config tftp:` toward SRV1 and receives `%Error opening tftp://10.1.1.100/R1-confg (Timed out)`. A `ping 10.1.1.100` from R1 succeeds. What is the most likely cause?
options: The TFTP service on SRV1 is not running, or a host firewall on SRV1 is dropping UDP port 69
R1 has no route to the 10.1.1.0/24 subnet, so the write request never leaves Gi0/0
The file `R1-confg` does not yet exist on SRV1, so the server refused the write request
The `ip ftp username` and `ip ftp password` commands are missing from R1's configuration
questions.explanation: `Timed out` means no TFTP reply arrived at all. The ping proves IP reachability, so the layer that failed is the service: TFTP is off, or UDP 69 is filtered on the server. A rejected request would produce a different error text.

whyWrong.1: The successful ping shows R1 can reach 10.1.1.100; it is a directly connected subnet anyway.
whyWrong.2: A TFTP write creates the file; a name problem would be reported by the server, not as a timeout.
whyWrong.3: TFTP has no credentials; the `ip ftp` commands matter only for `copy ftp:`.

questions.prompt: Which statement about SCP and SFTP on Cisco IOS XE is correct?
options: SFTP is FTP protected with TLS, while SCP is FTP protected with SSH
Both use TCP 21 for control and negotiate a separate data connection
Both use TCP 20 for data and need `ip ftp passive` when the router is behind NAT
Both run over SSH on TCP 22; the router can serve SCP but only acts as an SFTP client
questions.explanation: SCP and SFTP are two different protocols carried inside an SSH session on TCP 22. IOS XE can be an SCP server (`ip scp server enable`) and an SCP client, but SFTP support is client-side only (`copy sftp:`).

whyWrong.0: FTP over TLS is FTPS; SFTP is a separate SSH-based protocol and SCP is not FTP at all.
whyWrong.1: Ports 21 and a separate data connection describe FTP, not the SSH-based protocols.
whyWrong.2: Port 20 and `ip ftp passive` belong to FTP active/passive mode.

questions.prompt: An engineer upgrades an IOS router with these steps: (1) `copy tftp: flash:` to fetch the new image; (2) `boot system flash:new.bin`; (3) `copy running-config startup-config`; (4) `reload`. Which step is missing between steps 1 and 2?
options: `erase startup-config`, so the new image starts with a clean configuration
`verify /md5 flash:new.bin <published hash>`, to confirm the image is intact before booting from it
`config-register 0x2142`, so the router ignores the old boot variable at the next reload
`delete flash:old.bin`, because two IOS images cannot coexist in the same flash
questions.explanation: A completed transfer proves only that bytes arrived. Before pointing `boot system` at the file, `verify /md5` with the hash from cisco.com confirms the image is exactly what Cisco published; a corrupt image may leave the router in ROMMON.

whyWrong.0: Erasing the configuration is never part of an image upgrade.
whyWrong.2: `0x2142` ignores startup-config (including the `boot system` line); the register should stay `0x2102`.
whyWrong.3: Two images coexist fine if space allows, and keeping the old one is the usual fallback.

questions.prompt: After `copy running-config tftp:` completes successfully, what is true of the router's startup configuration?
options: It has been replaced by the copy that was just written to the server
It has been merged with the running configuration as part of the copy
It is unchanged; backing up the running configuration does not save it
It is cleared until the next `copy running-config startup-config`
questions.explanation: The copy reads `running-config` from RAM and writes it to the server. NVRAM is neither a source nor a destination, so `startup-config` stays as it was — unsaved changes are in the backup but will still be lost at a reload.

whyWrong.0: Only `copy running-config startup-config` (or `write memory`) writes NVRAM.
whyWrong.1: No merge occurs; merging is what happens when a file is copied *into* running-config.
whyWrong.3: Nothing clears NVRAM except `erase startup-config` / `write erase`.

cards.front: TFTP transport and port?
cards.back: UDP. The read/write request goes to port 69; the rest of the transfer uses ephemeral ports on both ends.

cards.front: TFTP block size and security?
cards.back: 512-byte blocks, one ACK per block. No username, no password, no encryption.

cards.front: FTP ports?
cards.back: TCP 21 for the control connection; TCP 20 is the server's source port for active-mode data.

cards.front: Active vs passive FTP?
cards.back: Active: the server opens the data connection to the client from port 20. Passive: the client opens it to a server-chosen high port. IOS default is active; `ip ftp passive` switches.

cards.front: Port used by SCP and SFTP?
cards.back: TCP 22 — both run inside an SSH session and inherit its encryption and authentication.

cards.front: Commands that store FTP client credentials on IOS?
cards.back: `ip ftp username <name>` and `ip ftp password <pass>` (global); or embed them: `ftp://user:pass@host/file`.

cards.front: Make an IOS router an SCP server?
cards.back: Working SSH + `aaa new-model` + `aaa authentication login default local` + `aaa authorization exec default local` + a privilege-15 user + `ip scp server enable`.

cards.front: SFTP role on IOS XE?
cards.back: Client only — `copy sftp://user@host/file bootflash:`; there is no SFTP server on the router.

cards.front: OpenSSH 9+ scp fails to IOS with `subsystem request failed`. Fix?
cards.back: Add `-O` (`scp -O …`) to force the legacy SCP protocol; modern scp uses SFTP by default.

cards.front: `copy tftp: running-config` — merge or replace?
cards.back: Merge: the file's commands are executed on top of the current config; commands absent from the file are not removed.

cards.front: `copy tftp: startup-config` — merge or replace, and what next?
cards.back: Replace: NVRAM is overwritten. Nothing changes in RAM until `reload` (answer **no** to the save prompt).

cards.front: Replace the running configuration from a file without a reload?
cards.back: `configure replace flash:<file>` — applies only the differences, including removals.

cards.front: Archive feature: sub-commands under `archive`?
cards.back: `path flash:<prefix>` · `write-memory` (snapshot on every save) · `time-period <min>` · `maximum <1–14>`. Restore with `configure replace`.

cards.front: Check an image against Cisco's published hash?
cards.back: `verify /md5 flash:<file> <hash>` — prints `Verified` or `%Error verifying`. Without the hash it just prints the computed MD5.

cards.front: Router has no `boot system` command. Which image boots?
cards.back: The first valid IOS image in flash (file 1 in `dir flash:`). `boot system` lines are tried in order and only after being saved.

cards.front: Configuration register 0x2102 vs 0x2142 vs 0x2100?
cards.back: 0x2102 normal boot. 0x2142 ignores startup-config (password recovery). 0x2100 stops in ROMMON.

cards.front: Config-register boot field values (low 4 bits)?
cards.back: 0 = ROMMON; 1 = first image in flash, ignoring boot system; 2–F = follow the boot system commands (default 2).

cards.front: Meaning of `*` and `#` in `show file systems`?
cards.back: `*` = default file system (bare filenames resolve here); `#` = the file system holding the boot image.

cards.front: Default filename offered by `copy running-config tftp:`?
cards.back: `<hostname>-confg` (for example `r1-confg`). Give it a dated name instead.

cards.front: IOS XE install-mode upgrade command and what it boots?
cards.back: `install add file bootflash:<image>.bin activate commit`; the device then boots `bootflash:packages.conf`. Bundle mode uses `boot system bootflash:<image>.bin`.

cards.front: `copy running-config startup-config` vs `copy startup-config running-config`?
cards.back: run → start saves RAM to NVRAM, replacing the saved configuration. start → run merges the saved configuration into the running one; commands added since the save are kept, not removed.

tickets.title: Golden config restored, but the 10.1.20.0/24 subnet is still blocked
tickets.scenario: During an incident an engineer added a temporary `deny` to access list 110 on R1 to isolate the 10.1.20.0/24 subnet. The incident is over. To undo every change at once, a colleague restored the known-good file `R1-golden.cfg` from the TFTP server. The restore reported success and the hostname and banner are correct, yet users in 10.1.20.0/24 still cannot reach anything through R1.

exhibits.text:
Extended IP access list 110
    5 deny ip 10.1.20.0 0.0.0.255 any (3412 matches)
    10 permit tcp 10.1.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
    20 permit ip 10.1.20.0 0.0.0.255 any

exhibits.title: R1# show logging | include CONFIG_I
exhibits.text:

%SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from tftp://10.1.1.100/R1-golden.cfg by admin on vty0 (10.1.1.50)

exhibits.text:
access-list 110 permit tcp 10.1.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
access-list 110 permit ip 10.1.20.0 0.0.0.255 any

tickets.question: Why is the temporary deny still in place after a successful restore?
options: The golden file on the TFTP server was corrupted, so only part of the access list was applied
The file was copied into running-config, which merges: its two permit lines already existed and nothing removed the deny at sequence 5
Numbered access lists cannot be restored from a text file; the list must be rebuilt by hand
R1 booted with configuration register 0x2142 and discarded the restored configuration
tickets.explanation: The log line `Configured from tftp://…/R1-golden.cfg` shows the file was applied to the **running** configuration, which is a merge. The file's two `access-list 110 permit` lines matched entries already present (sequence 10 and 20), so nothing changed, and the file contains no `no access-list 110` or `no 5 …` line to remove the troubleshooting entry. Sequence 5 stays at the top and keeps matching (3,412 hits). A restore that must remove commands has to replace, not merge.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1# copy tftp: startup-config
Address or name of remote host []? 10.1.1.100
Source filename []? R1-golden.cfg
Destination filename [startup-config]?
R1# reload
System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]: no
```
After the reload `show access-lists 110` starts at sequence 10. On a platform that supports it, `configure replace tftp://10.1.1.100/R1-golden.cfg` achieves the same without a reload.

tickets.title: IOS upgrade reload came back on the old image
tickets.scenario: An engineer staged `c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin` on R1 (a 2911) over SCP, verified its MD5 against cisco.com, entered `boot system flash:c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin`, and reloaded during the change window. The terminal log shows the reload prompt `System configuration has been modified. Save? [yes/no]:` answered with `no` because "only the boot line changed". After the reload the router is running the old release.

exhibits.title: R1# show version | include image|register
exhibits.text:
System image file is "flash0:c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.151-4.M4.bin"
Configuration register is 0x2102

exhibits.title: R1# dir flash:
exhibits.text:
Directory of flash0:/

    1  -rw-    33591768   Mar 1 1993 00:02:11 +00:00  c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.151-4.M4.bin
    2  -rw-    68491264   Sep 18 2026 09:40:12 +00:00  c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin

256487424 bytes total (154403038 bytes free)

exhibits.title: R1# show startup-config | include boot system

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: The new image failed its integrity check at boot, so the bootstrap fell back to the previous image
The configuration register must be 0x2101 before `boot system` commands are honoured
The `boot system` command was never saved, so the bootstrap found no boot commands and loaded the first image in flash
A 2911 always boots the first file in flash; the old image must be deleted before the new one can load
tickets.explanation: The bootstrap reads `boot system` commands from **startup-config**, and `show startup-config | include boot system` returns nothing — the line existed only in the running configuration, which was discarded when the save prompt was answered `no`. With boot field 2 and no boot commands the router loads the first image in flash, file 1, the old release. The register is the normal `0x2102` and the MD5 had already verified, so neither the image nor the register is at fault.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# boot system flash:c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin
R1(config)# boot system flash:c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.151-4.M4.bin
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config startup-config
R1# show bootvar
R1# reload
```
`show bootvar` now lists the new image first; after the reload `show version` reports `System image file is "flash0:c2900-universalk9-mz.SPA.154-3.M3.bin"`. The second `boot system` line keeps the old image as a fallback.

questions.prompt: A user's Windows 11 laptop cannot reach anything on the network. Based on the output, what happened?
options: A static address was typed into the wrong subnet, so the gateway line was left blank
DHCP is enabled but no server answered, so Windows self-assigned a link-local address
The DHCP server handed out 169.254.83.117 from a pool configured with a /16 mask
The adapter has no link, which is why Windows shows only an IPv6 link-local address
questions.explanation: `DHCP Enabled: Yes` plus the label **Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address** with a `169.254.x.x` address and a `255.255.0.0` mask is the APIPA signature: the client asked for a lease and nothing answered, so it picked a link-local address from `169.254.0.0/16`. The blank gateway and DNS lines follow from that.

whyWrong.0: `DHCP Enabled: Yes` rules out a static configuration.
whyWrong.2: No DHCP server hands out `169.254` addresses; the `Autoconfiguration` label means the client chose it itself.
whyWrong.3: An adapter with no link prints `Media State: Media disconnected` instead of any addresses.

questions.prompt: A host is configured as 10.1.20.57/24 with default gateway 10.1.20.254. The router's LAN interface is actually 10.1.20.1. Which pattern of results will the host show?
options: Nothing on the local subnet responds, but remote hosts by IP address still respond
Local and remote hosts respond by IP address, but every name lookup times out
Hosts on 10.1.20.0/24 respond, but every destination outside the subnet fails
Nothing responds at all until the host is released and renewed through DHCP
questions.explanation: The gateway is only used for destinations the mask says are remote. Local hosts are reached by ARP directly and work; every off-subnet packet is sent to 10.1.20.254, which does not exist, so those fail whether addressed by IP or by name.

whyWrong.0: This is backwards: a wrong gateway breaks remote, not local, traffic.
whyWrong.1: That is the wrong-DNS pattern; here the IP path to remote hosts is broken, so names and IPs both fail.
whyWrong.3: The address and mask are valid, so local communication works without any DHCP action.

questions.prompt: PC-A is configured as 192.168.40.10 with subnet mask 255.255.0.0 and default gateway 192.168.40.1. The router's interface is 192.168.40.1/24 and proxy ARP is disabled. Which destination can PC-A NOT reach?
options: 8.8.8.8, a public DNS server on the Internet
192.168.40.1, the router's LAN interface
172.16.5.5, a server in another building
192.168.50.10, a PC on another router interface
questions.explanation: With a /16 mask PC-A believes every `192.168.x.x` address is on its own link, so it ARPs for 192.168.50.10 directly instead of sending the packet to the gateway. Nobody on the LAN owns that address and proxy ARP is off, so the ARP request goes unanswered and the packet is never sent.

whyWrong.0: 8.8.8.8 is outside 192.168.0.0/16, so PC-A correctly forwards it to the gateway.
whyWrong.1: The gateway is inside both the real /24 and the wrong /16, so it is reachable either way.
whyWrong.2: 172.16.5.5 is outside 192.168.0.0/16 and is forwarded to the gateway normally.

questions.prompt: Which two Linux commands display the host's default gateway? (Choose two.)
options: ip route
ifconfig
nmcli device show
resolvectl status
ip link
questions.explanation: `ip route` prints the routing table, where the `default via` line names the gateway. `nmcli device show` prints a per-device summary that includes `IP4.GATEWAY` alongside addresses and DNS servers.

whyWrong.1: `ifconfig` shows addresses and masks but no routing information on any OS.
whyWrong.3: `resolvectl status` shows DNS resolvers, not routes.
whyWrong.4: `ip link` shows interface state and MAC addresses only.

questions.prompt: What subnet mask and prefix length is this Mac using on en0?
questions.explanation: macOS `ifconfig` prints the mask in hexadecimal. Each `f` is four one-bits, so `0xffffff00` is 24 one-bits followed by 8 zeros: `255.255.255.0`, a /24. The broadcast address `10.1.20.255` confirms it.

whyWrong.0: `0xffff0000` would be /16; this value has six `f`s, not four.
whyWrong.1: `0xffffffff` would be /32, and a /32 could not have a separate broadcast address.
whyWrong.3: `0xfffff000` would be /20; the value here ends in `ff00`, not `f000`.

exhibit.title: $ ip -br address; ip route
exhibit.text:
enp0s3           UP             10.1.20.59/24 fe80::a00:27ff:fe4e:66a1/64
default via 10.1.20.1 dev enp0s3 proto dhcp src 10.1.20.59 metric 100

questions.prompt: Which statement about this Linux host is correct?
options: Its address and default route were learned from DHCP, and off-subnet traffic goes to 10.1.20.1
Its address is static, because the output shows no lease time next to 10.1.20.59/24
It has no usable default gateway; only the connected 10.1.20.0/24 route is installed
It routes off-subnet traffic to 10.1.20.59, the address listed as src on both lines
questions.explanation: The `default via 10.1.20.1` line is the default route and `proto dhcp` on it means the route (and the address it was delivered with) came from a DHCP lease. `src 10.1.20.59` is merely the source address the host will use, not a next hop.

whyWrong.1: `ip -br address` never shows lease times; `proto dhcp` on the default route proves DHCP was used.
whyWrong.2: The first `ip route` line is exactly a default route via 10.1.20.1.
whyWrong.3: `src` names the host's own source address; the next hop is the address after `via`.

questions.prompt: A Windows client can ping its default gateway and 8.8.8.8, but `nslookup www.example.com` reports `DNS request timed out`. Which client parameter should you check first?
options: The subnet mask
The DNS server address
The default gateway
The DHCP server address
questions.explanation: A successful ping to 8.8.8.8 proves the address, mask and gateway are all correct — the IP path off the subnet works. Only name resolution fails, so the DNS server the client is configured to use is either wrong or unreachable.

whyWrong.0: A wrong mask would have broken some IP destinations, yet a remote IP address works.
whyWrong.2: The gateway is proven good by the ping to 8.8.8.8.
whyWrong.3: The DHCP server field only records who issued the lease; it does not affect name resolution.

questions.prompt: A Windows client still holds a stale lease after the DHCP server's pool was corrected. Which command sequence forces it to discard the lease and request a new one immediately?
options: `ipconfig /flushdns` then `ipconfig /registerdns`
`netsh wlan disconnect` then `netsh wlan connect`
`route delete 0.0.0.0` then `route add 0.0.0.0`
`ipconfig /release` then `ipconfig /renew`
questions.explanation: `ipconfig /release` sends a DHCP RELEASE and drops the address; `ipconfig /renew` starts a fresh DISCOVER/OFFER/REQUEST/ACK exchange so the client picks up the corrected pool settings.

whyWrong.0: Those commands clear and re-register DNS entries; they do not touch the lease.
whyWrong.1: Reconnecting Wi-Fi may trigger a renewal on a wireless adapter but does not release a wired lease, and it is not the DHCP command.
whyWrong.2: Editing the routing table changes the default route, not the leased address or lease state.

questions.prompt: A laptop must join a WPA2-Personal WLAN and then obtain a DHCP address. Which two client-side settings must match the WLAN exactly? (Choose two.)
options: The BSSID of the nearest access point
The SSID, including letter case
The channel the access point is using
The pre-shared passphrase
The access point's management IP address
questions.explanation: A WPA2-Personal client needs the exact SSID (case-sensitive, up to 32 characters), the matching security type, and the same 8–63 character passphrase. A wrong SSID means the network is never found; a wrong passphrase fails the 4-way handshake and the client never reaches DHCP.

whyWrong.0: The client learns BSSIDs by scanning and roams between them; it is never configured on the client.
whyWrong.2: Clients scan every channel; the channel is an AP setting, not a client parameter.
whyWrong.4: The AP's management address is invisible to the client and plays no part in association.

questions.prompt: The laptop shows connected to CORP-WLAN but cannot reach anything. What is the most likely cause?
options: The passphrase stored in the profile is wrong, so the 4-way handshake failed
The SSID in the profile differs in case from the one the access point advertises
Association succeeded, so the fault is in the DHCP path behind the access point
The profile uses CCMP while the access point requires the TKIP cipher
questions.explanation: `State: connected` with the intended SSID means the SSID, security type and passphrase all matched — the 4-way handshake completed. The `169.254` address with a `/16` mask shows the client then sent DHCP DISCOVERs and got no OFFER, so the fault lies in the VLAN, relay or DHCP server, not in the wireless settings.

whyWrong.0: A wrong passphrase never reaches `connected`; the client is deauthenticated and asked for the key again.
whyWrong.1: A wrong SSID would leave the client unable to find or join the network at all.
whyWrong.3: A cipher mismatch prevents association; the output shows association completed with CCMP.

questions.prompt: Which symptom points to a mistyped WPA2-Personal passphrase rather than a DHCP problem?
options: The client is repeatedly asked for the network security key and never shows connected
The client shows connected to the SSID but holds a 169.254.x.x address
The client shows connected with a valid address, but name lookups time out
The client sees the SSID in its scan list with a different security type
questions.explanation: With a wrong passphrase the client associates, then fails the 4-way handshake because the two sides derived different keys; the AP deauthenticates it and the OS prompts for the key again. The client never gets far enough to send a DHCP DISCOVER.

whyWrong.1: Connected plus APIPA means the wireless settings are right and DHCP failed afterwards.
whyWrong.2: A valid address with failing lookups is the wrong-DNS pattern.
whyWrong.3: A different advertised security type points to a security-type mismatch, not the passphrase.

questions.prompt: A Windows laptop has both its Ethernet and Wi-Fi adapters connected. Which gateway and interface will it use to reach 8.8.8.8?
options: 192.168.1.1 via 192.168.1.23, because that route is listed first
10.1.20.1 via 10.1.20.57, because its metric of 25 is lower
It alternates between the two default routes to balance the load
Neither; 8.8.8.8 matches an On-link route and is resolved by ARP
questions.explanation: Both `0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0` rows are default routes with the same prefix length, so Windows picks the one with the lowest metric. Metric 25 beats 50, so packets to 8.8.8.8 leave through 10.1.20.57 toward gateway 10.1.20.1.

whyWrong.0: Order in the table is not a tie-breaker; the metric is.
whyWrong.2: Windows does not load-balance between default routes of different metrics.
whyWrong.3: 8.8.8.8 does not fall inside either connected /24, so it needs a gateway.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an APIPA address is true?
options: It is assigned by the DHCP server as a fallback when the pool is exhausted
It can reach the Internet as long as the default gateway is on the same link
Linux NetworkManager assigns one by default whenever DHCP receives no offer
It comes from 169.254.0.0/16 with mask 255.255.0.0 and no default gateway
questions.explanation: APIPA (IPv4 link-local addressing) is chosen by the client itself from `169.254.0.0/16` when DHCP gets no answer. The mask is always `255.255.0.0` and no gateway or DNS server is set, so only other link-local hosts on the same segment are reachable.

whyWrong.0: No server is involved; APIPA exists precisely because the server did not answer.
whyWrong.1: There is no gateway with an APIPA address, so nothing off-link is reachable.
whyWrong.2: Linux normally leaves the interface with no IPv4 address; link-local is only used when explicitly configured.

spec.title: PC-A and the two servers
spec.caption: PC-A's configured parameters are shown under the PC; the DNS service runs on Server-A.

questions.prompt: PC-A opens http://192.168.50.20 successfully, but http://intranet.example fails with "server not found". Which single change fixes it?
options: Set PC-A's DNS server to 192.168.40.20
Set PC-A's default gateway to 192.168.40.20
Change PC-A's subnet mask to 255.255.0.0
Add a static route on PC-A for 192.168.50.0/24
questions.explanation: Reaching 192.168.50.20 by address proves the IP path — address, mask and gateway — is correct. Only the name fails, and PC-A is pointing at 192.168.40.99, which runs no DNS service. Pointing it at Server-A (192.168.40.20) fixes name resolution.

whyWrong.1: Server-A is not a router; the gateway .40.1 is already correct, as the successful IP access shows.
whyWrong.2: A /16 mask would make PC-A treat 192.168.50.20 as on-link and break the access that currently works.
whyWrong.3: Off-subnet traffic already reaches 192.168.50.20 through the gateway; routing is not the fault.

questions.prompt: On a Mac connected through a VPN, which command lists every DNS resolver in use, including resolvers scoped to specific domains?
options: `networksetup -listallhardwareports`
`route -n get default`
`scutil --dns`
`ifconfig -a`
questions.explanation: `scutil --dns` prints the system's full resolver configuration: each resolver's nameservers, search domains and, for VPN-supplied resolvers, the domains they are scoped to. It is the macOS equivalent of the DNS lines in `ipconfig /all`.

whyWrong.0: That command maps friendly names such as Wi-Fi to device names such as en0; it shows no DNS servers.
whyWrong.1: That shows the default gateway and its interface only.
whyWrong.3: `ifconfig` never shows DNS servers or routes on any OS.

cards.front: APIPA address range and mask?
cards.back: 169.254.0.0/16 with mask 255.255.0.0; no default gateway and no DNS server are set.

cards.front: What does a 169.254.x.x address on a DHCP client mean, and how does Windows label it?
cards.back: DHCP was enabled but no server answered, so the client self-assigned a link-local address. `ipconfig /all` labels it `Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address`.

cards.front: How does a Linux host show a failed DHCP lease?
cards.back: The interface is UP with no IPv4 address at all (only the fe80:: link-local IPv6). Linux does not fall back to APIPA by default.

cards.front: Windows command showing MAC, DHCP state, lease times, DHCP server and DNS servers?
cards.back: `ipconfig /all` (plain `ipconfig` shows only address, mask and gateway).

cards.front: Windows: force a new DHCP lease; clear the DNS cache?
cards.back: `ipconfig /release` then `ipconfig /renew`; `ipconfig /flushdns` (and `ipconfig /displaydns` to view the cache).

cards.front: Windows routing table command, and how the default route appears?
cards.back: `route print` (or `netstat -r`). The default route is the `0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0` row; with two default routes the lowest metric wins.

cards.front: Windows/macOS command to view the ARP cache, and what a gateway entry proves?
cards.back: `arp -a`. A `dynamic` entry for the gateway proves the router answered ARP — Layer 2 to the router is good.

cards.front: macOS ifconfig shows netmask 0xffffff00 — what mask is that?
macOS command for the default gateway?
cards.back: `route -n get default` (or the `default` row of `netstat -rn`). `ifconfig` never shows the gateway.

cards.front: macOS commands for DNS resolvers and for the DHCP-supplied settings of a service?
cards.back: `scutil --dns` (includes VPN-scoped resolvers); `networksetup -getdnsservers "Wi-Fi"`, `networksetup -getinfo "Wi-Fi"`, `ipconfig getpacket en0`.

cards.front: Linux commands for addresses and masks?
cards.back: `ip -br address` (brief) or `ip address show enp0s3`; the word `dynamic` after an address means it came from DHCP. `ifconfig` is legacy and may be missing.

cards.front: Linux command for the default gateway, and the line to look for?
cards.back: `ip route` — the `default via 10.1.20.1 dev enp0s3` line; `proto dhcp` means it came from the lease.

cards.front: Linux commands for DNS servers, and why /etc/resolv.conf can mislead?
cards.back: `resolvectl status` (systemd-resolved) or `nmcli device show`. On stub-mode systems resolv.conf only points at 127.0.0.53.

cards.front: Symptom of a wrong default gateway?
cards.back: Local subnet works, everything off-subnet fails by IP and by name. Windows: `Reply from <own IP>: Destination host unreachable.` (ARP for the gateway failed); `arp -a` has no gateway entry.

cards.front: Symptom of a wrong DNS server?
cards.back: `ping 8.8.8.8` and browsing by IP work; anything by name fails and `nslookup` times out.

cards.front: Symptom of a wrong subnet mask?
cards.back: Some destinations work, others fail, split at the wrong boundary. Too wide: the host ARPs for remote hosts instead of using the gateway. Too narrow: the gateway itself can fall outside the subnet. Proxy ARP on a Cisco router can hide it.

cards.front: Three wireless client settings that must match the WLAN?
cards.back: SSID (case-sensitive, up to 32 characters), security type (Open / WPA2-Personal / WPA3-Personal / Enterprise), passphrase (8–63 characters) for Personal.

cards.front: Symptom of a wrong WPA2-Personal passphrase?
cards.back: The client associates, the 4-way handshake fails, the AP deauthenticates it and the OS asks for the key again. It never sends DHCP DISCOVER. Check with `netsh wlan show interfaces`.

cards.front: Wireless client shows connected to the right SSID but has a 169.254 address — where is the fault?
cards.back: Not in the wireless settings: association completed. The DHCP path is broken (WLAN-to-VLAN mapping, missing ip helper-address, exhausted pool).

cards.front: Order of the client troubleshooting ladder?
cards.back: 127.0.0.1 → own address → default gateway (then `arp -a`) → remote IP → name (`nslookup`) → application. The first failing rung names the fault.

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: The DNS servers are unreachable from this subnet, so Internet names cannot be resolved
The static default gateway 10.1.20.254 does not exist, so ARP for it is never answered
The subnet mask is too narrow and places the router outside the PC's own subnet
The DHCP server had no free lease, so Windows fell back to the previous static address
tickets.explanation: `DHCP Enabled: No` says every value was typed by hand. The mask `255.255.255.0` matches the router's `/24`, and the file server on the local subnet works, so address and mask are fine. `ping 8.8.8.8` answers from the PC's **own** address with `Destination host unreachable` — the packet never left because ARP for the next hop failed — and `arp -a` confirms it: there is an entry for `10.1.20.20` but none for the configured gateway `10.1.20.254`. The gateway should be `10.1.20.1`. DNS was never tested, because no packet could reach `10.1.10.5` either.
tickets.fix:
```text

C:\> ping 10.1.20.1
C:\> arp -a
C:\> ping 8.8.8.8
C:\> nslookup www.example.com
```
Better still, return the PC to DHCP like its neighbours: `netsh interface ipv4 set address name="Ethernet" source=dhcp` and `netsh interface ipv4 set dnsservers name="Ethernet" source=dhcp`.

options: The laptops' saved profile holds the wrong passphrase, so the 4-way handshake never completes
The SSID in the laptops' profile differs in case from STAFF-WLAN, so they join a different WLAN
The VLAN 30 subinterface has no ip helper-address, so DHCP broadcasts never reach 10.1.10.5
The DHCP server's pool for 10.1.30.0/24 is exhausted, so the laptops fell back to APIPA

exhibit.title: R1# ping 10.0.20.10
exhibit.text:
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.0.20.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
.!!!!
Success rate is 80 percent (4/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/4 ms

questions.prompt: An engineer pings a server from a router for the first time since it booted and sees this output. What explains the first period?
options: R1 had no route to 10.0.20.10 until the first echo triggered a routing update
The first echo was discarded while R1 resolved the next hop's MAC address with ARP
An ACL on the path is rate-limiting ICMP to four packets per second
The first echo exceeded the path MTU and was silently fragmented
questions.explanation: IOS does not queue the first packet while ARP resolves the next hop; the echo is dropped and ARP completes in the meantime. The remaining four succeed, and a second run prints `!!!!!`. A single leading `.` with 80 % success is normal, not a fault.

whyWrong.0: A missing route produces `.....` on every echo, and pings do not trigger routing updates.
whyWrong.2: An ACL rate-limiting ICMP would drop packets throughout the run, not just the first one.
whyWrong.3: Fragmentation is silent and does not cause loss; an MTU problem with DF set prints `M`.

exhibit.title: R1# ping 10.0.50.1
exhibit.text:
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.0.50.1, timeout is 2 seconds:
U.U.U
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)

questions.prompt: R1's only path to 10.0.50.0/24 is a default route toward R2. What does this ping output prove?
options: The destination host 10.0.50.1 is up but is configured to ignore ICMP echo requests from R1
R1's outgoing interface toward R2 is down, so the five echoes never left the router at all
Some router on the path, most likely R2, returned ICMP destination unreachable for the echoes
The echoes reached 10.0.50.1 but each reply took longer than the 2-second timeout to return
questions.explanation: `U` means an ICMP destination unreachable message came back, so some router received the echo and refused to forward it. The alternating `U.U.U` pattern is IOS rate-limiting unreachables to one every 500 ms. Silence (`.....`) would point at a drop or a local problem instead.

whyWrong.0: A host that ignores echoes produces timeouts (`.`), not unreachables.
whyWrong.1: If R1's exit interface were down the default route would be withdrawn and R1 would print `.....`.
whyWrong.3: Late replies show as `.`; a `U` is a distinct ICMP error, not a slow echo reply.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe how IOS `traceroute` and Windows `tracert` differ? (Choose two.)
options: IOS traceroute sends UDP probes to destination ports starting at 33434
Windows tracert sends ICMP echo requests with an increasing TTL
IOS traceroute sends ICMP echo requests, exactly like Windows tracert
Windows tracert sends TCP SYN probes to port 80 by default
The destination answers an IOS traceroute with an ICMP echo reply
questions.explanation: IOS (and Linux by default) sends UDP datagrams to high ports from 33434 upward and expects ICMP port unreachable from the destination; Windows sends ICMP echo requests and expects an echo reply. Both rely on ICMP time exceeded from transit hops. The difference decides which trace a firewall permits.

whyWrong.2: IOS uses UDP probes, which is why an ACL permitting only ICMP breaks it.
whyWrong.3: TCP probes are a Linux `traceroute -T` option, not the Windows default.
whyWrong.4: An IOS trace ends when the destination returns ICMP port unreachable (type 3 code 3).

exhibit.title: R1# traceroute 203.0.113.10
exhibit.text:
Type escape sequence to abort.
Tracing the route to 203.0.113.10
  1 10.0.99.2 1 msec 1 msec 1 msec
  2 198.51.100.1 4 msec 4 msec 5 msec
  3  *  *  *
  4 203.0.113.1 9 msec 8 msec 9 msec
  5 203.0.113.10 10 msec 9 msec 10 msec

questions.prompt: A user reports that the web server 203.0.113.10 is slow. Based on this traceroute, which conclusion is valid?
options: Hop 3 is dropping user traffic, which explains why the server is slow for the user
The path is broken at hop 3, and hops 4 and 5 are being reached over a backup route
Hop 3 is congested and adds at least 3 seconds of delay to every packet that crosses it
Hop 3 forwards normally but does not send ICMP time-exceeded replies; the trace shows no fault
questions.explanation: Hops 4 and 5 answered promptly, so probes with TTL 4 and 5 passed through hop 3 without trouble. Three stars at a hop that later hops follow mean that router filters or rate-limits its own ICMP replies — a common ISP policy. The trace shows nothing wrong with the path.

whyWrong.0: If hop 3 dropped traffic, hops 4 and 5 could not have replied.
whyWrong.1: There is no backup route in play; the same forwarding path carried the later probes.
whyWrong.2: Stars are timeouts of the reply, not delay on the forwarding path; the 9 ms at hop 4 shows the path is fast.

questions.prompt: Users behind R1 lost the WAN this morning. Which cause is consistent with the state of Gi0/1?
options: An engineer entered `shutdown` under interface Gi0/1 on R1
The IP address on Gi0/1 overlaps with another interface's subnet
A cable fault, a shutdown far-end port, or a speed mismatch
The two ends of the link are using different Layer 2 encapsulations
questions.explanation: `down/down` means no usable signal at Layer 1: no cable, a dead far end, a `shutdown` on the neighbour, or a speed mismatch. A `shutdown` on R1 itself would print `administratively down`, as Gi0/2 does. Check the cable and the neighbour's interface.

whyWrong.0: A local `shutdown` shows `administratively down`, which is what Gi0/2 displays.
whyWrong.1: Addressing is a Layer 3 matter; `down/down` reports a missing Layer 1 signal, which no IP address can cause.
whyWrong.3: An encapsulation mismatch gives `up/down` — Layer 1 works but line protocol fails.

exhibit.text:

  ...
  Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is 10/100BaseTX
  ...

questions.prompt: Fa0/24 connects SW1 to router R1, whose interface is configured with `speed 100` and `duplex full`. Transfers through the link are slow. What is the cause?
options: A duplex mismatch: R1 is hard-set, so SW1 falls back to half duplex and counts late collisions
A faulty cable: late collisions are counted when the FCS of received frames fails
Congestion: the link carries more traffic than 100 Mbps and the excess is dropped
A speed mismatch: SW1 sensed 100 Mbps but R1 is actually running at 1000 Mbps
questions.explanation: When one end is hard-set, it stops negotiating; the auto end senses the speed but defaults to half duplex. The half-duplex side counts collisions and **late collisions** on a link that should have none, while the full-duplex side shows CRC errors and runts. Set SW1 Fa0/24 to `speed 100` and `duplex full`, or return both ends to auto.

whyWrong.1: Cabling faults show as CRC and frame errors on input; here input errors are zero.
whyWrong.2: Congestion shows as `Total output drops`, not as collisions, and the link would still be full duplex.
whyWrong.3: A speed mismatch keeps the link `down/down`; this link is `up/up`.

spec.title: PC-A cannot reach SRV; R1 can
spec.caption: R1's plain ping to SRV succeeds; PC-A's ping to SRV fails.

questions.prompt: PC-A can ping 10.0.10.1 but not 10.0.20.10. On R1, `ping 10.0.20.10` succeeds. The engineer then runs an extended ping from R1 to 10.0.20.10 with source address 10.0.10.1 and it fails. What does the failed extended ping most likely indicate?
options: R1's Gi0/0 interface is down, so packets sourced from 10.0.10.1 cannot be sent
R2 or SRV lacks a route back to 10.0.10.0/24, which the plain ping could not test
PC-A has the wrong default gateway, so its echoes never leave its own subnet
R1 has no route to 10.0.20.0/24 and is dropping the sourced ping locally
questions.explanation: A plain ping from R1 uses the exit interface address `10.0.99.1`, which R2 is directly connected to, so the reply always finds its way back. Sourcing the ping from `10.0.10.1` makes the reply need a route to `10.0.10.0/24` on R2 — exactly what PC-A's traffic needs. Its failure isolates the return path.

whyWrong.0: PC-A can ping 10.0.10.1, so Gi0/0 is up and IOS would refuse to source from a down interface anyway.
whyWrong.2: The extended ping is sent by R1, not PC-A, and it failed as well, so the fault lies beyond R1 whatever PC-A's settings are.
whyWrong.3: The plain ping to 10.0.20.10 succeeded, so R1 has a route to that subnet.

exhibit.text:
*Mar  1 09:10:42.311: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down
*Mar  1 09:10:43.311: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to down

questions.prompt: R1 is configured with `logging host 10.0.20.10` and `logging trap warnings`. Which of these two messages reached the syslog server?
options: Only the %LINK-3-UPDOWN message, because severity 3 is more severe than the warnings threshold
Only the %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN message, because level 5 is above the warnings threshold
Both messages, because `logging trap` sends every message the buffer receives
Neither message, because link-state changes are logged to the console only
questions.explanation: `logging trap warnings` sends severity 4 (warnings) and every more severe level — 3, 2, 1, 0 — to the syslog server. `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` is severity 3 and is sent; `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN` is severity 5 (notifications), which is less severe than 4 and is filtered out.

whyWrong.1: Lower numbers are more severe; level 5 is *less* severe than the level-4 threshold and is not sent.
whyWrong.2: `logging trap` takes a level and sends only that level and lower numbers; the buffer has its own level.
whyWrong.3: Link-state messages go to every destination whose level admits them: console, buffer, monitor and syslog.

questions.prompt: A user cannot open the application on port 8080 of server 10.0.20.10. Given this capture, what is the most likely cause?
options: A firewall between the two hosts is silently dropping the SYN before it reaches the server
The server is unreachable from the client because R2 has no route back to 10.0.10.0/24
The client's advertised window of 64240 bytes is too small for the server to accept the connection
The server received the SYN and refused it: nothing listens on 8080 or its host firewall rejects it
questions.explanation: A `RST, ACK` from the server's own address in reply to a `SYN` proves the packet arrived and the host actively refused the connection. Network reachability is therefore fine; the fault is on the server (service stopped, wrong port) or in its host firewall. A silent drop would show the SYN retransmitted with no reply.

whyWrong.0: A silent drop produces retransmitted SYNs and no reply; here the server answered.
whyWrong.1: The reply came from 10.0.20.10, so routing in both directions works.
whyWrong.2: Window size never causes a reset; it only governs how much unacknowledged data may be in flight.

questions.prompt: A user reports that `app.corp.example` "is down". What does this capture show?
options: The DNS server 10.0.20.10 is unreachable, so the client's query timed out
The DNS server answered but could not complete the lookup because of an upstream failure
The DNS server replied NXDOMAIN: it is reachable, but the name does not exist
The name resolved correctly but the application server rejected the connection
questions.explanation: `No such name` is Wireshark's rendering of RCODE 3, NXDOMAIN. The query reached the server and a reply came back 3 ms later, so connectivity and the resolver are fine; the record is missing or misspelled. This is a data problem for the DNS administrator, not a network fault.

whyWrong.0: A timeout would show the query repeated with no response line at all.
whyWrong.1: An upstream failure produces `Server failure` (SERVFAIL, RCODE 2), not `No such name`.
whyWrong.3: No address was returned, so no connection to the application was ever attempted.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about using `show mac address-table` and `show arp` during a fault walk are correct? (Choose two.)
options: IOS router ARP entries age out after 300 seconds by default
An `Incomplete` ARP entry means the router sent ARP requests but got no reply
The switch MAC address table ages dynamic entries after 4 hours by default
A DYNAMIC MAC entry on an unexpected port or VLAN reveals a moved or mis-patched host
A MAC entry in the switch table proves the host's IP address and mask are correct
questions.explanation: The MAC table records where the switch last saw each source MAC and in which VLAN, so a PC that appears on the wrong port or VLAN has been moved or mis-patched. On the router, `Incomplete` means the router asked and nobody answered — the host is off, in another VLAN, or has a different address.

whyWrong.0: The IOS ARP timeout is 4 hours (`04:00:00` in `show interfaces`); 300 s is the MAC table aging time.
whyWrong.2: The MAC table ages after 300 seconds; 4 hours is the ARP timeout.
whyWrong.4: The MAC table is Layer 2 only; a host with a wrong IP address still populates it.

questions.prompt: PC-A (10.0.10.50) cannot ping 10.0.40.10. R1's next hop toward that network is R2 at 10.0.99.2. What does the capture prove?
options: An ACL on R2 denied the echo and R2 returned ICMP type 3 code 13

The host 10.0.40.10 is down, so R2 could not resolve its MAC address
The echo's TTL of 127 expired at R2, which returned ICMP time exceeded
questions.explanation: `Communication administratively filtered` is ICMP type 3 code 13, which a Cisco router sends when an ACL denies a packet (unless `no ip unreachables` is set). The source `10.0.99.2` identifies R2 as the router that applied the ACL. Check `show access-lists` and `show ip interface` on R2.

whyWrong.1: A missing route produces `Network unreachable` (type 3 code 0), a different text.
whyWrong.2: A failed ARP produces `Host unreachable` (code 1) from the router on the host's LAN.
whyWrong.3: TTL 127 has many hops left, and a TTL expiry is type 11, shown as `Time-to-live exceeded`.

questions.prompt: You suspect a WAN link has a small MTU. From R1, which command sends 500 echoes of 1500 bytes to 10.0.20.10, sourced from 10.0.10.1, that fail rather than fragment?
options: `ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 500 size 1500 df-bit`
`ping 10.0.20.10 from 10.0.10.1 count 500 length 1500 no-fragment`
`ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 500 mtu 1500 dont-fragment`
questions.explanation: IOS one-line extended ping uses the keywords `source`, `repeat`, `size` and `df-bit`. With the DF bit set, any link whose MTU is below 1500 returns ICMP fragmentation needed and the ping prints `M` instead of silently fragmenting. Add `sweep` in the interactive dialog to find the exact MTU.

whyWrong.1: `from`, `count`, `length` and `no-fragment` are not IOS ping keywords.
whyWrong.2: That is the Windows syntax (`-S`, `-n`, `-l`, `-f`), not IOS.
whyWrong.3: `mtu` and `dont-fragment` are not IOS ping keywords; the size keyword is `size` and the DF keyword is `df-bit`.

questions.prompt: A ticket says a PC cannot reach a file server. The engineer's first action is to ping the server from the PC, planning to look at cabling and VLANs if it fails and at DNS and the application if it succeeds. Which troubleshooting approach is this?
options: Bottom-up, because the ping tests the physical path first
Follow-the-path, because the ping walks every hop to the server
Top-down, because the engineer starts with the user's application
Divide-and-conquer, because a Layer 3 test decides whether to look above or below it
questions.explanation: Divide-and-conquer starts in the middle of the stack — usually with a ping — and lets the result decide the direction: success clears Layers 1–3 and sends you up; failure sends you down. It is the fastest opener for a generic connectivity ticket.

whyWrong.0: Bottom-up starts at the cable and link lights, not with a Layer 3 test.
whyWrong.1: Follow-the-path checks each hop's routing and ARP in turn; a single end-to-end ping does not.
whyWrong.2: Top-down starts by testing the application itself, then works downward.

questions.prompt: Users on Fa0/3 and Fa0/4 have no connectivity. Which pair of actions addresses both ports?
options: Replace the cables on Fa0/3 and Fa0/4; both statuses indicate a Layer 1 fault
For Fa0/3 read `show logging` for the violation, fix it and bounce the port; for Fa0/4 create VLAN 30 on SW1

whyWrong.3: Err-disable recovery applies to Fa0/3, not Fa0/4, and err-disabled is not a speed negotiation failure.

cards.front: IOS `ping` defaults: how many echoes, what size, what timeout?
cards.back: 5 echoes of 100 bytes, 2-second timeout, sourced from the exit interface.

cards.front: IOS ping codes: `!` `.` `U` `Q` `M` `?` `&`
cards.back: `!` reply · `.` timeout · `U` destination unreachable · `Q` source quench · `M` could not fragment · `?` unknown packet type · `&` TTL exceeded.

cards.front: Why does the first IOS ping to a new destination often print `.`?
cards.back: The first echo is dropped while ARP resolves the next hop's MAC; the rest succeed (`.!!!!`). Not a fault.

cards.front: `.` versus `U` in a ping — what is the difference?
cards.back: `.` is silence (dropped somewhere, no reply); `U` is a refusal — a router sent ICMP destination unreachable (no route or ACL).

cards.front: One-line extended ping: source, 100 repeats, 1500 bytes, DF set
cards.back: `ping 10.0.20.10 source 10.0.10.1 repeat 100 size 1500 df-bit`

cards.front: What does an extended ping with a `source` address prove?
cards.back: The return path: the remote device must have a route back to the source subnet, just as user traffic needs.

cards.front: IOS `traceroute`: probe type, port, probes per hop, max hops
cards.back: UDP probes to destination ports starting at 33434, 3 probes per TTL, up to 30 hops, 3 s timeout.

cards.front: Windows `tracert` vs Linux `traceroute` probes
cards.back: Windows sends ICMP echo requests; Linux defaults to UDP (33434+), `-I` for ICMP, `-T` for TCP SYN.

cards.front: Which ICMP messages does a traceroute rely on?
cards.back: Transit hops: time exceeded (type 11). Destination: port unreachable (type 3 code 3) for UDP traces; echo reply for Windows.

cards.front: Traceroute codes: `*` `!H` `!N` `!P` `!A` (Linux `!X`)
cards.back: `*` timeout · `!H` host unreachable · `!N` network unreachable · `!P` protocol unreachable · `!A`/`!X` administratively prohibited.

cards.front: `* * *` at hop 3 but hops 4–5 answer: what does it mean?
cards.back: Hop 3 forwards but does not send ICMP time-exceeded (filtered/rate-limited). Not a fault. Stars to the end = packet dies there.

cards.front: Interface pairs: down/down, administratively down/down, up/down
cards.back: down/down = Layer 1 (cable, far end shut, speed mismatch); administratively down = your `shutdown`; up/down = Layer 2 (serial encapsulation/keepalive).

cards.front: `show interfaces status` states: connected, notconnect, disabled, err-disabled, inactive
cards.back: connected = up/up · notconnect = no link · disabled = shutdown · err-disabled = violation · inactive = access VLAN does not exist.

cards.front: Duplex mismatch: which counters on which side?
cards.back: Half-duplex side: collisions and late collisions. Full-duplex side: CRC errors and runts. Link stays up/up; CDP logs `%CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH`.

cards.front: runts, giants, late collision, Total output drops — meanings
cards.back: runts < 64 bytes · giants > 1518 bytes · late collision = collision after byte 64 (duplex mismatch/long cable) · output drops = congestion.

cards.front: Default aging: IOS ARP table vs switch MAC table
cards.back: ARP entries 4 hours (04:00:00); dynamic MAC entries 300 seconds.

cards.front: Syslog severities 0–7 by name
cards.back: 0 emergencies · 1 alerts · 2 critical · 3 errors · 4 warnings · 5 notifications · 6 informational · 7 debugging.

cards.front: Format of an IOS log message and what `logging trap 4` sends
cards.back: `%FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: text`. A level sends that level and all lower numbers (more severe), so trap 4 sends 0–4.

cards.front: See log/debug output in an SSH session; stop a runaway debug
cards.back: `terminal monitor` (EXEC). `undebug all` or `no debug all`.

cards.front: Capture: a SYN is answered by RST, ACK from the server — versus no reply at all?
cards.back: RST, ACK = the SYN reached the host and it refused (nothing listening on that port, or a host firewall rejects it). No reply, SYN retransmitted = dropped on the path.

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: R1's Gi0/1 was shut down by an unlogged configuration change on R1
A speed mismatch between R1 Gi0/1 and R2 Gi0/1 brought the link down
R2's Gi0/1 was administratively shut down at 09:10:41, taking the link down at both ends
The static default route on R1 was removed, so R1 stopped forwarding toward R2
tickets.explanation: R1 shows `down/down`, not `administratively down`, so the fault is not R1's configuration. R1's log times the failure at 09:10:42 with `%LINK-3-UPDOWN`. R2's log, one second earlier, says `%LINK-5-CHANGED ... administratively down` — the message IOS logs only for a `shutdown`. Someone on R2 shut the interface; the missing route on R1 is a consequence, not the cause.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2# configure terminal
R2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# end
R2# show ip interface brief
```

tickets.question: Why do the users fail while R1's plain ping succeeds?
options: R1's default route is wrong, so packets from 10.0.10.0/24 are sent to the wrong next hop
R2 has no route back to 10.0.10.0/24; R1's plain ping worked only because it was sourced from 10.0.99.1, which R2 is connected to
SRV has a host firewall that permits ICMP from routers but denies it from PCs
An ACL on R2 Gi0/1 denies traffic from 10.0.10.0/24 and returns unreachables to R1
tickets.explanation: The plain ping from R1 uses `10.0.99.1` as its source, and R2 is directly connected to that subnet, so the reply always returns. The extended ping sourced from `10.0.10.1` fails with silence, and R2's routing table confirms why: no `10.0.10.0/24` entry and no gateway of last resort. The PC's tracert reaches R1 and then hears nothing, because the time-exceeded replies from R2 onward have no route back either.

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the slow transfers?
options: A duplex mismatch: R1 Gi0/0 is hard-set to full duplex and no longer negotiates, so SW1 Fa0/24 fell back to half duplex and suffers late collisions
A bad patch cable on Fa0/24 producing CRC errors that force TCP to retransmit
A speed mismatch: SW1 negotiated 100 Mbps while R1 runs at 1000 Mbps, causing drops
Congestion on the trunk: the collisions counter shows the link is saturated
tickets.explanation: `a-half` on SW1 means it auto-negotiated and landed on half duplex, which happens when the other end is hard-set and sends no negotiation. The half-duplex side counts collisions and **late collisions** on a link that should have none, while input errors and CRC stay at zero — cabling is fine. CDP confirms it in words: `not full duplex` here, `full duplex` on R1. Pings survive because small packets rarely collide; large transfers do not.
tickets.fix:
```ios
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# interface fastethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# speed 100
SW1(config-if)# duplex full
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# clear counters fastethernet0/24
SW1# show interfaces fastethernet0/24 | include duplex|late
```

questions.prompt: A branch router still accepts SNMP requests using the default community string `public`. Which term correctly describes this condition?
options: A threat, because the string is publicly known
A vulnerability, because it is a weakness an attacker could use
An exploit, because SNMP can read the configuration
A mitigation, because read-only SNMP limits the damage
questions.explanation: A **vulnerability** is a weakness in a system. A default community string is exactly that: a condition that an attacker could take advantage of. The *possibility* that someone reads the configuration is the threat, and the act of doing so with `snmpwalk` is the exploit.

whyWrong.0: A threat is the potential harm, not the weakness that makes the harm possible.
whyWrong.2: An exploit is the method or tool used against a weakness, not the weakness itself.
whyWrong.3: A mitigation reduces risk; leaving a default credential in place does the opposite.

questions.prompt: R1 is configured with `login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60`, yet it never entered quiet mode during this activity. Which attack best matches the log, and why did the lockout not trigger?
options: A brute-force attack on the admin account; the attacker's tool retried too slowly for the counter to notice
A dictionary attack; `login block-for` only counts failures on the console line
Password spraying; one attempt per account every 15 minutes never produces 3 failures within 60 seconds
Credential stuffing; the leaked pairs were valid so no failure was ever counted
questions.explanation: One source is trying **many different usernames**, once each, roughly 15 minutes apart. That is **password spraying**: a few common passwords across many accounts, paced deliberately to stay under the lockout threshold. Three failures never fall inside the 60-second window, so quiet mode is never entered.

whyWrong.0: Brute force hammers one account with many passwords; here each username appears only once.
whyWrong.1: `login block-for` watches VTY and other remote logins; these attempts arrive on port 22.
whyWrong.3: Credential stuffing replays known-good pairs; every attempt here failed, so no valid credential was used.

spec.title: Captured at the ISP edge
spec.caption: Thousands of these exchanges per second, toward hundreds of different resolvers.

questions.prompt: Server B's internet link is saturated with DNS responses it never requested. Which attack does the exhibit show, and what makes it effective?
options: Reflection and amplification — the source is forged as the victim and the replies dwarf the requests
A SYN flood — the resolver holds a half-open connection for every query it receives
A man-in-the-middle attack — the resolver sits between Host A and Server B
DNS cache poisoning — the forged queries corrupt the cache on Server B
questions.explanation: Host A forges the **source address** as Server B, so every resolver *reflects* its reply onto B. The `ANY` query is 64 bytes and the reply is 3,200 bytes — a 50× **amplification** — so a modest attacker link becomes a flood at the victim, delivered by servers that were never compromised.

whyWrong.1: DNS here is UDP; there is no handshake and no half-open state to exhaust.
whyWrong.2: The resolver is not intercepting a conversation between two parties; it is simply answering forged queries.
whyWrong.3: Cache poisoning injects false records into a resolver; this attack fills the victim's link with volume.

questions.prompt: Which two features mitigate Layer 2 attacks on a Catalyst access switch? (Choose two.)
options: Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding on the uplink
DHCP snooping with the uplink as the only trusted port
SYN cookies on the switch management interface
Dynamic ARP Inspection on the user VLANs
TCP intercept on the default gateway
questions.explanation: **DHCP snooping** stops rogue DHCP servers by dropping server messages on untrusted ports and builds the binding table that **Dynamic ARP Inspection** uses to drop forged ARP replies. Both operate on the access switch against Layer 2 attacks (DHCP spoofing, ARP poisoning).

whyWrong.0: uRPF checks Layer 3 source addresses on routers; it does nothing about DHCP or ARP forgery.
whyWrong.2: SYN cookies defend a TCP server against SYN floods, a Layer 4 attack.
whyWrong.4: TCP intercept is a router/firewall SYN-flood defence, not a switch feature.

questions.prompt: During a TCP SYN flood, which resource on the target server is exhausted first?
options: The table of half-open connections awaiting the final ACK
The bandwidth of the server's uplink
The DNS resolver cache on the server
The server's ARP cache entries for the attackers
questions.explanation: The server replies SYN-ACK to every forged SYN and keeps a **half-open connection** entry while it waits for an ACK that never comes. The backlog fills, and genuine SYNs are dropped. SYN cookies avoid storing that state.

whyWrong.1: SYNs are tiny; the attack exhausts connection state long before it fills the link.
whyWrong.2: DNS is not involved in a SYN flood.
whyWrong.3: Forged sources are usually off-subnet; the server's ARP cache holds only its gateway.

questions.prompt: Overnight, malware spreads from one file server to twelve others by exploiting an unpatched SMB service. Nobody opened a file or ran a program. Which malware type is this?
options: A virus, because it copied itself into other programs
A trojan horse, because it arrived disguised as a service
A worm, because it self-propagates through a vulnerability
Ransomware, because it targets file servers specifically
questions.explanation: A **worm** spreads on its own across the network by exploiting a vulnerability, with no user action. That is exactly the described behaviour, and it is why patching is the primary defence against worms.

whyWrong.0: A virus attaches to a file or program and needs a user to run it.
whyWrong.1: A trojan is installed deliberately by a user who believes it is useful software.
whyWrong.3: Ransomware describes the payload (encrypting data for payment), not this spreading mechanism.

questions.prompt: An employee receives a voicemail claiming to be from the company's bank, asking them to call a number back and confirm their card PIN. Which social-engineering variant is this?
options: Smishing
Pharming
Spear phishing
Vishing
questions.explanation: **Vishing** is phishing over voice — a call or voicemail that impersonates a trusted party to extract secrets such as PINs or one-time codes.

whyWrong.0: Smishing uses SMS text messages, not voice.
whyWrong.1: Pharming redirects a correctly typed URL to a fake site through DNS tampering; no message is involved.
whyWrong.2: Spear phishing is a targeted email; the channel here is voice.

spec.title: VLAN 10 after a laptop joined Fa0/7
spec.caption: PC1's ARP cache now maps 10.0.10.1 to aaaa.bbbb.cccc, which is the laptop's MAC, not R1's.

questions.prompt: Users on VLAN 10 report that the internet became slow after a visitor's laptop was plugged into Fa0/7. The exhibit shows what a capture on PC1 revealed. Which switch feature prevents this attack?
options: BPDU guard on Fa0/7
Port security with a maximum of one MAC address
Dynamic ARP Inspection on VLAN 10
Root guard on the uplink toward R1
questions.explanation: The laptop is sending forged ARP replies that bind the gateway's IP to its own MAC — **ARP spoofing**, the classic LAN man-in-the-middle. **Dynamic ARP Inspection** checks every ARP reply on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops the forgery.

whyWrong.0: BPDU guard stops rogue switches sending spanning-tree BPDUs; the laptop is sending ARP, not BPDUs.
whyWrong.1: The laptop uses a single, genuine MAC address, so port security sees nothing wrong.
whyWrong.3: Root guard protects the spanning-tree root role; it does not inspect ARP.

enable password 7 0822455D0A16
username admin password 7 094F471A1A0A

questions.prompt: A copy of this router's configuration was found on a shared drive open to all staff. What can someone who reads it do?
options: Nothing useful — type 7 is a one-way hash like type 5
Recover every password in seconds — type 7 is reversible encoding
Recover only the line password; the enable and username strings use a stronger scheme
Recover the passwords only if they also obtain the router's encryption key
questions.explanation: `service password-encryption` produces **type 7** strings, a reversible Vigenère-style encoding that any online decoder undoes instantly. All three credentials here are type 7, so the whole management plane is exposed. The fix is `enable secret` and `username ... secret`, which store salted hashes (type 5, 8 or 9).

whyWrong.0: Type 7 is not a hash; only `secret` lines (types 5, 8, 9) are one-way.
whyWrong.2: All three lines are marked `7`; none of them uses a stronger scheme.
whyWrong.3: Type 7 uses a fixed, publicly known key — nothing else is needed.

questions.prompt: Which login combination is genuine multifactor authentication?
options: A password and a four-digit PIN
A password and the answer to a security question
A username and a long passphrase
A password and a code from an authenticator app
questions.explanation: MFA requires evidence from two **different categories**. A password is something you *know*; the authenticator app runs on a phone you *have*. Stealing the password alone is not enough.

whyWrong.0: A PIN is another knowledge secret — same category as the password.
whyWrong.1: A security question is also something you know.
whyWrong.2: A username is an identifier, not a factor; the passphrase is the only factor.

questions.prompt: Which two statements correctly describe elements of a password policy? (Choose two.)
options: Complexity sets the minimum number of days between password changes
History prevents a user from reusing any of their last N passwords
Expiry requires a password to be changed once it reaches a maximum age
Lockout limits the number of characters a password may contain
Length specifies how many failed attempts disable the account
questions.explanation: **History** keeps the last N passwords and refuses their reuse; **expiry** (maximum age) forces a change after a set period. Length sets the minimum characters, complexity sets required character classes, lockout sets the failed-attempt threshold, and minimum age sets the shortest time between changes.

whyWrong.0: That is minimum age; complexity is about character classes.
whyWrong.3: Lockout concerns failed attempts; length concerns characters.
whyWrong.4: Length is a character count; lockout is the failed-attempt count.

Only the source that failed three times is blocked; the admin's client has a stale SSH key
SSH is disabled until the RSA key pair is regenerated
questions.explanation: `login block-for` puts the router into **quiet mode** after the failure threshold, and quiet mode denies logins from **all sources** unless a `login quiet-mode access-class` ACL exempts them. No ACL is configured here, so the administrator is refused for the remaining 87 seconds.

whyWrong.1: Per-user lockout is a separate AAA feature; `show login` reports line-level quiet mode, not a locked account.
whyWrong.2: The output says *all sources*; quiet mode is not per-source without an ACL.
whyWrong.3: Nothing here concerns SSH keys; the service is up and simply refusing logins.

questions.prompt: Once a month the IT team sends staff a realistic but harmless phishing email and shows anyone who clicks a short page explaining what they missed. Which security-program element is this?
options: Physical access control
User awareness
Acceptable-use policy enforcement
User training
questions.explanation: Simulated phishing with immediate feedback keeps the threat in people's minds and sharpens their suspicion at the moment it matters — that is **user awareness**. It is light, continuous and broad, unlike formal training.

whyWrong.0: Physical access control concerns doors, racks and badges.
whyWrong.2: An acceptable-use policy states rules; the exercise measures and improves behaviour rather than enforcing a rule.
whyWrong.3: Training is a formal, assessed session that teaches specific skills; a monthly reminder campaign is awareness.

questions.prompt: A contractor entered a secure data centre by walking in behind an employee who politely held the door. Which physical control addresses this specific attack?
options: A CCTV camera recording the entrance lobby
A locked rack for the core switches
A cable lock on each server chassis
A turnstile that admits one badge holder at a time
questions.explanation: This is **tailgating**. A mantrap or turnstile admits exactly one authenticated person per badge, so nobody can follow an employee through without their own credential.

whyWrong.0: A camera detects and records the tailgating but does not prevent it.
whyWrong.1: A locked rack protects equipment after the intruder is already inside the room.
whyWrong.2: Cable locks stop theft of a device; they do not control entry.

questions.prompt: What does a client actually prove when it authenticates using a digital certificate?
options: That it knows the certificate authority's private key
That it possesses the private key matching the CA-signed public key
That its certificate file is unique on the network
That it has a valid password stored inside the certificate
questions.explanation: A certificate binds a name to a **public key** and is signed by a trusted **CA**. Authentication is a challenge the client can answer only with the matching **private key**, which never leaves the device — so no shared secret is typed or transmitted.

whyWrong.0: The CA's private key stays with the CA; it signs certificates, it is never shared with clients.
whyWrong.2: Certificates are public documents; uniqueness proves nothing about identity.
whyWrong.3: Certificates contain no passwords; they replace them.

cards.front: Vulnerability?
cards.back: A weakness in a system: default password, unpatched service, open port, unlocked cabinet, over-permissive ACL.

cards.front: Exploit?
cards.back: The method or tool that takes advantage of a vulnerability: a script, a crafted packet, a phishing email, logging in with the default password.

cards.front: Threat vs threat actor?
cards.back: Threat = the potential harm (an exploit used against a vulnerability). Threat actor = the person or program that would do it.

cards.front: Mitigation?
cards.back: A control that removes the vulnerability, blocks the exploit or reduces the impact: patch, ACL, hashed secret, lock, backup.

cards.front: CIA triad — what each protects, typical control?
cards.back: Confidentiality (encryption, ACLs) · Integrity (hashes, signatures, change control) · Availability (redundancy, DoS protection, backups).

cards.front: SYN flood — what does it exhaust and what defends it?
cards.back: The server's half-open TCP connection backlog (SYN-ACK sent, ACK never arrives). Defences: SYN cookies, TCP intercept, rate limiting.

cards.front: Reflection vs amplification?
cards.back: Reflection: source forged as the victim so third-party servers reply to it. Amplification: the reply is far larger than the request (DNS ANY, NTP monlist).

cards.front: Virus vs worm vs trojan horse?
cards.back: Virus attaches to a program and needs a user to run it; worm self-propagates through a vulnerability; trojan is malware disguised as useful software.

cards.front: Spear phishing / whaling / vishing / smishing / pharming?
cards.back: Spear = targeted person; whaling = executive target; vishing = voice call; smishing = SMS; pharming = DNS tampering sends a correctly typed URL to a fake site (no message sent).

cards.front: Brute force / dictionary vs password spraying vs credential stuffing?
cards.back: Brute/dictionary: many passwords against one account. Spraying: one or two passwords against many accounts (dodges lockout). Stuffing: replaying leaked username/password pairs.

cards.front: Layer 2 attack → mitigation (5 pairs)?
cards.back: MAC flooding → port security · DHCP spoofing → DHCP snooping · ARP poisoning → DAI · VLAN hopping → no DTP + unused native VLAN · STP attack → BPDU guard / root guard.

cards.front: LAN man-in-the-middle — the classic method and its fix?
cards.back: ARP spoofing: gratuitous ARP claims the gateway's IP is at the attacker's MAC. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection (plus DHCP snooping, encryption end-to-end).

cards.front: Password policy elements (name six)?
cards.back: Length (IOS: `security passwords min-length` 0–16), complexity, expiry (max age), history, lockout, minimum age — plus hashed storage and management (unique per system, password manager, remove on leaving).

cards.front: Three MFA factor categories with an example each?
cards.back: Something you know (password, PIN) · something you have (token, authenticator app, smart card, certificate) · something you are (fingerprint, face, iris).

cards.front: Is password + PIN multifactor?
cards.back: No — both are knowledge factors. Password + authenticator-app code (know + have) is MFA.

cards.front: What does certificate authentication prove?
cards.back: Possession of the private key that matches the public key in a certificate signed by a trusted CA. No shared secret is typed or sent.

cards.front: Biometrics — two error rates and the big limitation?
cards.back: False acceptance rate (impostor admitted) vs false rejection rate (right person refused). A leaked fingerprint cannot be changed.

cards.front: User awareness vs user training?
cards.back: Awareness: continuous reminders that keep people alert (phishing simulations, posters). Training: formal, assessed sessions that teach specific skills.

cards.front: IOS password storage types 0 / 5 / 7 / 8 / 9?
cards.back: 0 cleartext · 5 salted MD5 (`enable secret`) · 7 reversible (`service password-encryption`) · 8 PBKDF2-SHA256 · 9 scrypt.

cards.front: `login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60` — meaning?
cards.back: After 3 failed logins within 60 s, enter quiet mode for 120 s: all logins refused unless a `login quiet-mode access-class` ACL permits the source.

commands.task: Require every password or secret configured from now on to be at least 10 characters.
commands.note: Range 0–16. Checked on enable secret/password, username and line passwords entered afterwards.

commands.note: Stored as type 5 (salted MD5) on IOS 15. Overrides enable password if both exist.

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the administrators' lockouts?
options: The admin account is locked by `aaa local authentication attempts max-fail` and must be cleared by hand
An internet host is guessing passwords on the VTY lines; each burst triggers quiet mode, which denies every source including the management subnet
The RSA key pair has expired, so SSH sessions are rejected until it is regenerated
`exec-timeout 5 0` drops idle administrator sessions, and each drop is counted as a failed login
tickets.explanation: The log shows a public address (`203.0.113.44`) cycling through default usernames on port 22 — a **password-guessing** attack from the internet. Every three failures inside 60 seconds trip `login block-for`, and `show login` confirms **`Denying logins from all sources`** with **no quiet-mode ACL**, so administrators are refused along with the attacker. Two vulnerabilities combine here: the VTY lines are reachable from the internet (no `access-class`), and quiet mode has no exemption for management addresses.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1(config)# ip access-list standard MGMT
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit 10.0.99.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-std-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# login quiet-mode access-class MGMT
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# access-class MGMT in
R1(config-line)# end
R1# show login
```
The `access-class` refuses the internet host before it reaches a password prompt, so no further failures are logged and quiet mode stops triggering. The quiet-mode ACL guarantees that `10.0.99.0/24` can still log in if quiet mode is ever entered again. Keep `login block-for`; it is doing its job.
