tickets.question: How did the attacker obtain a working credential without triggering any failure or lockout?
options: `service password-encryption` was never applied to the copied file, so the backup held the passwords in cleartext
The copied configuration contained type 7 strings, which are reversible; the attacker decoded the admin and enable passwords and simply logged in
The attacker brute-forced the account; `login on-failure log` was not configured, so the failures were never recorded
A rogue DHCP server redirected an administrator's SSH session through a man in the middle that captured the password
tickets.explanation: The configuration stores both the enable password and the admin account with **`password 7`** — the reversible encoding produced by `service password-encryption`. Anyone with the leaked file decodes them in seconds and logs in with a **valid** credential, which produces a `LOGIN_SUCCESS` and zero failures; `login block-for` never sees anything to block. The vulnerability is weak credential storage combined with an insecure backup; the exploit is a type 7 decoder; the threat was realised by whoever read the share.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2(config)# no enable password
R2(config)# enable secret N3w-Enable-2026!
R2(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret N3w-Adm1n-2026!
R2(config)# ip access-list standard MGMT
R2(config-std-nacl)# permit 10.0.99.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config-std-nacl)# exit
R2(config)# line vty 0 4
R2(config-line)# access-class MGMT in
R2(config-line)# end
R2# show running-config | include secret
```
Rotate every credential that appeared in the leaked file (including any SNMP community or routing-protocol key), audit what the intruder changed, and move configuration backups to an access-controlled store. `secret` lines are salted hashes (type 5, or type 8/9 with `algorithm-type` on IOS 15.3(3)M+); type 7 must be treated as cleartext.

questions.prompt: An engineer logs in to a switch with a valid username and password. She can run `show` commands, but `configure terminal` returns `Command authorization failed`. The central server records the attempt. Which AAA function denied the `configure terminal` command?
options: Authentication, because the account is limited to user EXEC mode
Accounting, because the server logged the command as a violation
Authorization, because the policy for her identity does not permit that command
Authentication, because the enable secret was never entered
questions.explanation: Authentication already succeeded — the credentials were accepted. Deciding what an authenticated identity may do is **authorization**, and a per-command check that says no is exactly that. Recording the attempt is accounting.

whyWrong.0: Authentication only proves identity; it does not decide which commands are allowed.
whyWrong.1: Accounting records what happened; it never permits or denies anything.
whyWrong.3: The message is a command-authorization result, not a missing enable password.

exhibit.title: R1# show running-config | section aaa|username|line vty
exhibit.text:
aaa new-model
line vty 0 4
 password cisco
 transport input ssh

questions.prompt: Before `aaa new-model` was added, engineers opened SSH to R1 with the vty password. Now every SSH attempt is refused. Based on the output, why?
options: With no login list defined, the vty lines now check the local database, and no `username` exists
`aaa new-model` disables SSH until a TACACS+ or RADIUS server group is defined
The `transport input ssh` command conflicts with AAA and must be re-entered after `aaa new-model`
The `password cisco` line was invalidated because AAA requires `secret` instead of `password`
questions.explanation: `aaa new-model` moves every line to the `default` login method list and removes `login`/`login local`. With no default list configured, IOS checks the local username database — which is empty here — so no SSH login can succeed. Add a `username` or a proper `aaa authentication login default` list.

whyWrong.1: AAA works with `local` alone; no server group is required.
whyWrong.2: `transport input ssh` is unaffected by AAA; SSH is still listening.
whyWrong.3: The line `password` is simply no longer consulted; its syntax is not the problem.

questions.prompt: Which transport protocol and port does TACACS+ use for authentication, authorization and accounting?
options: UDP 1812 for authentication and UDP 1813 for accounting
UDP 1645 for authentication and UDP 1646 for accounting
TCP 1812 for all three functions
TCP 49 for all three functions
questions.explanation: TACACS+ runs over **TCP port 49** and uses that one port for authentication, authorization and accounting, each as a separate exchange.

whyWrong.0: 1812/1813 are the current RADIUS ports, and RADIUS uses UDP.
whyWrong.1: 1645/1646 are the legacy RADIUS ports.
whyWrong.2: TACACS+ does use TCP, but its port is 49, not 1812.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about RADIUS are true? (Choose two.)
options: It uses UDP, with 1812 for authentication and 1813 for accounting
It encrypts the entire body of every packet between NAS and server
It uses TCP port 49 for authentication, authorization and accounting
It obscures only the password; the other attributes are sent in clear
It can authorize each individual command an administrator types
questions.explanation: RADIUS is a UDP protocol on ports 1812/1813 (legacy 1645/1646). Its Access-Request obscures only the User-Password attribute; the username, NAS address and all returned attributes are readable on the wire.

whyWrong.1: Whole-body encryption is a TACACS+ property.
whyWrong.2: TCP 49 is TACACS+.
whyWrong.4: Per-command authorization needs separate authorization exchanges, which only TACACS+ has.

exhibit.title: R1# show running-config | include aaa authentication
exhibit.text: aaa authentication login default group ISE-TAC local

questions.prompt: The TACACS+ server in group ISE-TAC is reachable. A user opens SSH to R1 and types a password that the server does not accept. What does R1 do next?
options: Checks the local username database and accepts the login if the password matches there
Refuses the login; the local database is not consulted because the server answered
Retries the server twice more, then checks the local database
Falls back to the enable secret because no `enable` method is listed
questions.explanation: A method list moves to the next method only on an **ERROR** (no reply). A reachable server that rejects the password returns **FAIL**, which ends the attempt. Otherwise central policy could be bypassed with a stale local password.

whyWrong.0: That would let anyone rejected by the server try a local password; IOS does not do this.
whyWrong.2: Retransmission applies when there is no answer, not to a rejection.
whyWrong.3: `enable` is used only if it appears in the list, and only after an ERROR.

spec.title: Login attempt on R1
spec.caption: R1 is configured with aaa authentication login default group ISE-TAC local.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows a login on R1, whose default login list is `group ISE-TAC local`. Why did the user get a prompt even though the server never answered?
options: TACACS+ retransmits over TCP until the server responds, so the login was queued
The console list applies to SSH sessions when a server is unreachable
`aaa new-model` allows any login when no server responds
The group returned an ERROR after the timeout, so IOS tried the next method, `local`
questions.explanation: No reply within the 5-second timeout is an **ERROR**, and an ERROR is the one condition that moves a method list to its next method. The local database accepted the `admin` account.

whyWrong.0: After the timeout the server is treated as unavailable; the login is not queued.
whyWrong.1: Named console lists apply only to the line they are bound to.
whyWrong.2: AAA never grants access by default; a method must accept the user.

questions.prompt: An engineer created the list `aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group ISE-TAC local`. Which command, in line configuration mode for `vty 0 4`, makes SSH sessions use it?
options: `aaa authentication VTY-AUTH`
`login local VTY-AUTH`
`login authentication VTY-AUTH`
`authorization exec VTY-AUTH`
questions.explanation: A named login list does nothing until a line binds it with `login authentication NAME`. Lines without that command use the `default` login list.

whyWrong.0: `aaa authentication` commands are global, not line commands.
whyWrong.1: `login local` is removed once `aaa new-model` is enabled and takes no list name.
whyWrong.3: `authorization exec` binds an authorization list, not an authentication list.

questions.prompt: Users report that SSH logins to R1 pause for several seconds and then only local accounts work. What does the output indicate?
options: The server is not answering, so logins fall back to `local` after the timeout
The server is rejecting the users' passwords, so logins fall back to `local` at once
The server group is missing from the login list, so no requests are ever sent
Command accounting is enabled for RADIUS, which delays each login by the timeout
questions.explanation: Six of nine authentication requests **timed out** and the state is DOWN: R1 sent requests and got no reply. That is the ERROR path — the list falls back to `local` after the timeout, which matches the pause. Rejections would be answered transactions, not timeouts.

whyWrong.1: A rejection is a reply; it would not count as a timeout.
whyWrong.2: If the group were not in the list, R1 would send no requests at all.
whyWrong.3: This is a TACACS+ entry and the counters concern authentication, not accounting.

questions.prompt: A router is configured with `radius-server host 10.0.0.100 key R4dius-Key` and no port keywords. To which UDP ports does it send authentication and accounting requests?
options: 49 and 49
questions.explanation: The legacy `radius-server host` command defaults to the original RADIUS ports, **1645** for authentication and **1646** for accounting. To use the standard pair, add `auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813`, and always check that the ports match what the server listens on.

whyWrong.0: 1812/1813 are the IETF-assigned ports, but `radius-server host` uses them only when `auth-port` and `acct-port` say so.
whyWrong.2: 49 is the TACACS+ port.
whyWrong.3: The two legacy ports go together; the router does not mix the pairs.

questions.prompt: A security team wants administrators' every configuration command checked against a central policy before it runs on the device. Which two facts make TACACS+ the right protocol? (Choose two.)
options: It runs over UDP, so each command check adds no connection overhead
It separates authorization from authentication, so each command can be checked
It returns all of the user's permissions inside the authentication reply
It is the protocol switches use for 802.1X port-based authentication
It encrypts the whole packet body, so the command strings are hidden on the wire
questions.explanation: Per-command authorization exists because TACACS+ separates authorization from authentication and can be queried for every command. Since the entire body is encrypted, those command strings are not exposed on the network. RADIUS combines authorization with the Access-Accept and cannot check individual commands.

whyWrong.0: TACACS+ uses TCP port 49.
whyWrong.2: Returning permissions inside the authentication reply is how RADIUS works.
whyWrong.3: 802.1X uses RADIUS; TACACS+ is the device-administration protocol.

exhibit.title: R1# show running-config | section aaa
exhibit.text:
aaa new-model
aaa group server tacacs+ ISE-TAC

aaa authentication login default group ISE-TAC local

questions.prompt: The TACACS+ server is down for maintenance. Administrators can authenticate to R1 with local accounts, but the session immediately closes with `% Authorization failed`. Which change fixes this while the server is down?
options: Add `aaa authorization console` so local users are authorized
Remove `local` from the login list so both lists use the same method
Append `local` to the `aaa authorization exec default` list
Add `aaa accounting exec default start-stop group ISE-TAC`
questions.explanation: Login falls back to `local` because that list has a second method; the exec authorization list has only the server group, so when it returns ERROR there is nothing left and authorization fails. Adding `local` (privilege from the `username` line) or `if-authenticated` gives the list a method that can succeed.

whyWrong.0: `aaa authorization console` only extends authorization to the console line; it adds no method.
whyWrong.1: Removing `local` from the login list would stop logins from working as well.
whyWrong.3: Accounting records sessions; it does not authorize them.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) is correct?
options: It is a RADIUS-only server, so device administration must use a separate TACACS+ product
It is a TACACS+-only server intended for CLI administration of Cisco devices
It runs on the router itself and replaces the local username database
It is an AAA server that supports RADIUS for network access and TACACS+ for device administration
questions.explanation: ISE is Cisco's AAA server. It speaks RADIUS for network access (802.1X, wireless, VPN, guest) and, since ISE 2.0, TACACS+ for device administration, taking over both roles from the older ACS.

whyWrong.0: ISE added TACACS+ device administration in version 2.0.
whyWrong.1: ISE's largest role is RADIUS-based network access control.
whyWrong.2: ISE is a separate server; the router is its AAA client.

aaa authentication login default group ISE-TAC local
aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
line con 0

questions.prompt: The TACACS+ server becomes unreachable. Which statement describes console and SSH logins on R1 while it is down?
options: Console and SSH both refuse every login until the server returns
Console logins use the local database immediately; SSH logins use it after the server timeout
Console logins wait for the server timeout; SSH logins use the local database immediately
Console logins succeed without a password; SSH logins use the local database
questions.explanation: The console is bound to the named list `CONSOLE`, whose only method is `local`, so it never contacts the server. The vty lines use `default`, which tries the group first; when the group returns ERROR after the timeout, `local` is used.

whyWrong.0: Both lists end in `local`, so both work while the server is down.
whyWrong.2: It is the reverse: the console list has no server in it.
whyWrong.3: Password-free console access only happens when no default list exists at all; here `CONSOLE local` is bound.

questions.prompt: An auditor wants a record on the TACACS+ server whenever an administrator's EXEC session begins and again when it ends. Which command meets the requirement?
options: `aaa accounting exec default start-stop group ISE-TAC`
`aaa accounting exec default stop-only group ISE-TAC`
`aaa authorization exec default group ISE-TAC local`
`aaa accounting commands 15 default stop-only group ISE-TAC`
questions.explanation: `start-stop` sends an accounting record when the session starts and another when it stops; `exec` is the type for EXEC shells. `stop-only` would produce one record at the end.

whyWrong.1: `stop-only` sends a single record when the session ends, not at the start.
whyWrong.2: Authorization decides whether the shell is allowed; it records nothing.
whyWrong.3: Command accounting records individual commands, not session start and end.

cards.front: The three A's of AAA, in one word each?
cards.back: Authentication = prove identity; Authorization = what is permitted; Accounting = record what happened.

cards.front: TACACS+ transport and port?
cards.back: TCP port 49 — one port for authentication, authorization and accounting.

cards.front: RADIUS ports (current and legacy)?
cards.back: UDP 1812 authentication/authorization, UDP 1813 accounting; legacy UDP 1645/1646.

cards.front: Which protocol encrypts the entire packet body?
cards.back: TACACS+ (only the 12-byte header is in clear). RADIUS hides only the password.

cards.front: Which protocol combines authentication and authorization in one reply?
cards.back: RADIUS — the Access-Accept carries the authorization attributes. TACACS+ keeps them as separate exchanges.

cards.front: Which protocol supports per-command authorization?
cards.back: TACACS+ only. RADIUS cannot check individual commands.

cards.front: Typical use: TACACS+ vs RADIUS?
cards.back: TACACS+ = device administration (CLI access). RADIUS = network access (802.1X, wireless, VPN).

cards.front: Which of TACACS+ and RADIUS is Cisco-developed, and which is an open standard?
cards.back: TACACS+ was developed by Cisco. RADIUS is an open IETF standard with broad multivendor support.

cards.front: Cisco's AAA server product?
cards.back: Cisco ISE (Identity Services Engine) — RADIUS for network access and TACACS+ for device administration; replaced ACS.

cards.front: In AAA terms, which device is the client?
cards.back: The router/switch (the NAS) is the AAA client of the server, even though it is the SSH server for the administrator.

cards.front: What does `aaa new-model` do to the lines immediately?
cards.back: All lines use the default login method list; `login`/`login local` are removed. No default list defined = local database (console lets you in unchecked).

cards.front: When does a method list move to the next method?
cards.back: Only on ERROR (no server answered). A FAIL (server rejected the user) ends the attempt — local is not tried.

cards.front: Command: default login list = TACACS+ group ISE-TAC, then local?
cards.back: `aaa authentication login default group ISE-TAC local`

cards.front: Bind a named login list to the vty lines?
cards.back: `line vty 0 4` → `login authentication NAME`

cards.front: Modern syntax to define a TACACS+ server?
cards.back: `tacacs server NAME` → `address ipv4 A.B.C.D` → `key SECRET`. RADIUS: `radius server NAME` → `address ipv4 A.B.C.D auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813` → `key SECRET`.

cards.front: Legacy one-line server commands and their RADIUS port defaults?
cards.back: `tacacs-server host A.B.C.D key K`; `radius-server host A.B.C.D key K` — defaults to UDP 1645/1646 unless `auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813` is given.

cards.front: Build a server group and add a named server?
cards.back: `aaa group server tacacs+ NAME` → `server name SERVER` (RADIUS: `aaa group server radius NAME`).

cards.front: Accounting keywords `start-stop` vs `stop-only`?
cards.back: `start-stop` = record at session/command start and end; `stop-only` = one record at the end. Command accounting is TACACS+ only.

cards.front: Test a server from the router, and see server counters?
cards.back: `test aaa group NAME user pass legacy` (or `new-code`); `show aaa servers` (watch timeouts); `show tacacs`.

cards.front: Default TACACS+/RADIUS server timeout, and does exec authorization apply to the console?
cards.back: 5 seconds. No — not unless `aaa authorization console` is configured.

tickets.title: Nobody can SSH to the branch router since the security change
tickets.scenario: A junior engineer was asked to "turn on AAA" on branch router BR1 in preparation for a TACACS+ rollout next month. Since the change, every engineer who opens SSH to BR1 is prompted for a username, which never happened before, and no password works. The engineer says he only added one line and did not touch the vty configuration. The console still works.

exhibits.title: BR1# show running-config | section aaa|username|line vty
exhibits.text:
aaa new-model
line vty 0 4
 password cisco
 transport input ssh

exhibits.title: BR1# show running-config | include enable
exhibits.text: enable secret 5 $1$mERr$hx5rVt7rPNoS4wqbXKX7m0

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: `transport input ssh` must be re-applied after `aaa new-model` because the line was reset
`aaa new-model` moved the vty lines to the default login list, which uses the local database — and there is no local username
The enable secret is stored as a type 5 hash, which AAA cannot read
SSH requires a TACACS+ server group to be defined once `aaa new-model` is enabled
tickets.explanation: The only change was `aaa new-model`. That command removes `login` from the lines and makes every line use the `default` login method list; with no default list configured, IOS checks the local `username` database. The first exhibit shows no `username` line at all, so every SSH login fails. The console still works because, with no default list defined, the console lets you in without a check. The vty `password` is no longer consulted.
tickets.fix:
```ios
BR1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret Loc4l-Only!
BR1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
BR1(config)# aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
BR1(config)# line console 0
BR1(config-line)# login authentication CONSOLE
```

tickets.title: TACACS+ was rolled out, but logins still use the local accounts
tickets.scenario: Router R2 was configured as a TACACS+ client of the new ISE deployment. The ISE administrator reports that R2 has never sent a single authentication request, yet engineers can still log in with the old local accounts and are logged in instantly, with no delay. `ping 10.0.0.100` from R2 succeeds and the shared key has been double-checked.

exhibits.title: R2# show running-config | section aaa|tacacs
exhibits.text:
aaa new-model
tacacs server ISE1
 address ipv4 10.0.0.100
 key 7 0822455D0A16544541
aaa group server tacacs+ ISE-TAC
 server name ISE1
aaa authentication login default local
aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group ISE-TAC local

exhibits.title: R2# show running-config | section line vty
exhibits.text:
line vty 0 4
 transport input ssh

exhibits.title: R2# show aaa servers | include Authen
exhibits.text: Authen: request 0, timeouts 0, failover 0, retransmission 0

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: The named list VTY-AUTH was never applied to the vty lines, so they use the `default` list, which is `local`
The shared key is stored encrypted (type 7), so it no longer matches the key on ISE
The server group refers to `server name ISE1` but the block is a `tacacs server`, which needs `server 10.0.0.100`
TACACS+ requests are being sent but ISE is dropping them because TCP 49 is blocked
tickets.explanation: The vty lines show no `login authentication VTY-AUTH`, so they use the `default` login list — and that list is `local`. Every login is answered instantly from the local database and no request is ever sent: `show aaa servers` confirms `request 0`. If TCP 49 were blocked, requests would be counted and would time out, and logins would pause for the timeout before falling back.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R2(config)# line vty 0 4
R2(config-line)# login authentication VTY-AUTH
```

exhibit.title: R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
exhibit.text:
Extended IP access list CLIENTS-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq www (48 matches)
    15 permit icmp host 10.100.10.10 host 10.100.20.20 echo (4 matches)
    20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 (8 matches)
    30 permit ip any any (112 matches)

questions.prompt: CLIENTS-IN is applied inbound on R1's G0/0, which connects the 10.100.10.0/24 LAN. PC-B (10.100.10.11) pings 10.100.20.20. Which entry processes PC-B's echo request?
options: Sequence 10 — ICMP rides inside IP and the destination host matches the entry
Sequence 15 — it is the only entry in the list that names the ICMP protocol
Sequence 20 — entry 15 names only host .10, so 20 is the first entry that fits
Sequence 30 — permit ip any any is the entry that catches every protocol
questions.explanation: The router checks entries top-down and stops at the first match. Entry 10 requires TCP, entry 15 requires source `10.100.10.10`, so PC-B's ICMP packet from `.11` to `.20` first fits entry 20 and is denied; entry 30 is never consulted.

whyWrong.0: Entry 10 matches only the `tcp` protocol with destination port 80; an ICMP packet does not fit it.
whyWrong.1: Entry 15 matches only source host 10.100.10.10; PC-B is .11.
whyWrong.3: Entry 30 would match, but evaluation stopped at entry 20 — the first match wins.

questions.prompt: Which wildcard mask matches exactly the addresses in 172.16.32.0/20 and nothing else?
questions.explanation: A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0. Subtracting from 255.255.255.255 gives `0.0.15.255`: the block size in the third octet is 16, so the wildcard octet is 16 − 1 = 15, and the fourth octet is fully ignored.

whyWrong.1: 16 is the block size, not the wildcard; the wildcard octet is block size minus one.
whyWrong.2: 0.0.31.255 is the wildcard for a /19 — twice as many addresses.
whyWrong.3: 0.0.255.255 matches the whole /16.

questions.prompt: A router has the entry `access-list 20 permit 192.168.16.0 0.0.7.255`. Which range of source addresses does it permit?
questions.explanation: Wildcard 7 in the third octet means a block of 8 values starting at 16, so third octets 16–23 match, and 255 in the fourth octet means every host. That is `192.168.16.0`–`192.168.23.255`, eight consecutive /24s.

whyWrong.0: That is what 0.0.0.255 would match — a single /24.
whyWrong.1: 16–31 would need a wildcard of 0.0.15.255.
whyWrong.2: The block starts at the address given (16), not at 0.

questions.prompt: Which two numbers can identify a standard IPv4 ACL on a Cisco router? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Standard IPv4 ACLs use `1–99` and the expanded range `1300–1999`. Extended ACLs use `100–199` and `2000–2699`. 99 and 1400 fall in the standard ranges.

whyWrong.1: 150 is in the extended range 100–199.
whyWrong.3: 2300 is in the expanded extended range 2000–2699.
whyWrong.4: 199 is the top of the extended range 100–199.

exhibit.title: R1# show running-config | include access
exhibit.text:
access-list 101 permit ip any any
access-list 101 deny tcp any host 10.100.20.30 eq 22
 ip access-group 101 in

questions.prompt: The administrator intends to block SSH to 10.100.20.30 while permitting all other traffic, and has applied ACL 101 inbound on the LAN interface. Users report they can still SSH to the server. What is wrong?
options: The deny entry needs the established keyword to catch SSH sessions
The permit ip any any is evaluated first and matches every packet, so the deny is never reached
Extended ACLs must be applied outbound, so nothing is filtered inbound on that interface
SSH must be written as eq ssh; the numeric port 22 is not matched by IOS
questions.explanation: ACLs are evaluated top-down and stop at the first match. `permit ip any any` is the first entry and matches every IPv4 packet, including SSH to the server, so the more specific deny below it never sees a packet. The deny must come first.

whyWrong.0: `established` matches ACK/RST segments; it would exclude the initial SYN, the opposite of what is needed.
whyWrong.2: Extended ACLs may be applied in either direction; inbound on the source LAN is the recommended placement.
whyWrong.3: IOS matches numeric port numbers, and 22 is the SSH port.

questions.prompt: An administrator enters `ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in` on G0/0 before creating any entries in the named ACL CLIENTS-IN. What happens to traffic entering G0/0?
options: Everything is dropped by the implicit deny at the end of the list
Only packets addressed to the router itself are dropped
The router refuses the ip access-group command until the list has an entry
Everything is permitted — an ACL with no entries does not filter at all
questions.explanation: IOS accepts the reference to a list that does not exist or has no entries, and such a list permits all traffic. The implicit deny only takes effect once the list contains at least one entry. This is why a misspelt ACL name in `ip access-group` silently disables filtering.

whyWrong.0: The implicit deny applies only to a list that has at least one entry.
whyWrong.1: There is no special handling for router-addressed packets in an empty list.
whyWrong.2: IOS accepts the command without checking that the list exists.

exhibit.title: PC1 reaches SRV across three routers

spec.title: LAN A to LAN C
spec.caption: PC1 and PC2 share LAN A behind R1; SRV is alone on LAN C behind R3.

questions.prompt: A standard ACL must stop PC1 (10.1.1.10) from reaching SRV (10.3.3.30) while leaving all of PC1's other traffic untouched. Where should the ACL be applied?
options: R1 G0/0, inbound — as close to the source as possible
R1 G0/1, outbound — on the WAN link toward R2
R3 G0/1, outbound — on the interface facing SRV
R3 G0/0, inbound — on the WAN link from R2
questions.explanation: A standard ACL matches only the source address, so wherever it is applied it blocks PC1 from *everything* beyond that point. Applying it outbound on R3 G0/1 limits the effect to LAN C, which holds only SRV — closest to the destination.

whyWrong.0: Inbound on R1 G0/0 the list would block PC1 from every destination beyond R1.
whyWrong.1: Outbound on the WAN link blocks PC1 from everything behind R2 and R3.
whyWrong.3: Inbound on R3 G0/0 still blocks PC1 from any other network R3 might reach; G0/1 out is closer to SRV.

exhibit.title: PC1 reaches SRV across three routers

spec.title: LAN A to LAN C
spec.caption: PC1 and PC2 share LAN A behind R1; SRV is on LAN C behind R3.

questions.prompt: An extended ACL must block only Telnet (TCP 23) from PC1 to SRV. Following Cisco's placement guideline, where should it be applied?
options: R1 G0/0, inbound — closest to the source
R3 G0/1, outbound — closest to the destination
R2 G0/0, inbound — in the middle so both directions are covered
R1 G0/1, inbound — where the return traffic enters R1
questions.explanation: An extended ACL can name the exact flow (source, destination, protocol, port), so it is placed as close to the source as possible: inbound on R1 G0/0 the unwanted packets are dropped before crossing either WAN link.

whyWrong.1: Closest to the destination is the guideline for *standard* ACLs, which cannot identify the flow.
whyWrong.2: R2 is not close to the source, and one ACL in one direction does not cover both directions anyway.
whyWrong.3: The Telnet requests from PC1 leave R1 through G0/1; only replies enter there.

exhibit.title: R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0 | include access list
exhibit.text:
Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is not set

R1# show access-lists
Extended IP access list CLIENTS-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq www
    20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
    30 permit ip any any

questions.prompt: CLIENTS-IN was written to filter packets arriving from the LAN on G0/0, but traffic is unaffected and no counter ever increments. Based on the output, what is the cause?
options: The entries are in the wrong order, so permit ip any any always matches first
The ACL was never applied to G0/0 with ip access-group, so it filters nothing
The ACL is applied outbound, but LAN traffic enters G0/0 inbound
Counters are disabled until clear access-list counters is run once
questions.explanation: `show ip interface` reports both directions as `not set`, so no list is attached to G0/0. An ACL that exists in the configuration but is not applied with `ip access-group` is just a stored policy — it matches nothing and its counters stay empty.

whyWrong.0: The order is correct (specific entries above the general permit); an ordering fault would still produce counters on entry 30.
whyWrong.2: Both `Outgoing` and `Inbound` say `not set`; nothing is applied in either direction.
whyWrong.3: Counters run from the moment a list is applied; clearing only resets them.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about the `established` keyword in an extended ACL are true? (Choose two.)
options: It can be used in tcp, udp and icmp entries of an extended ACL
It matches segments with ACK or RST set, so a session's opening SYN does not match
It makes the router track the state of each session like a stateful firewall
It is typically used to permit return traffic for inside-initiated sessions
It must be combined with the log keyword before it takes effect
questions.explanation: `established` is a TCP flag test: a segment matches when ACK or RST is set, which is every segment of a conversation except the opening SYN. Placed inbound on an outside interface, it lets replies to inside-initiated sessions through while blocking outside-initiated connections.

whyWrong.0: It is valid only after the `tcp` keyword; UDP and ICMP have no such flags.
whyWrong.2: It inspects flags packet by packet and keeps no session table.
whyWrong.4: `log` only adds syslog messages; it has nothing to do with matching.

exhibit.title: R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
exhibit.text:
Extended IP access list CLIENTS-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq www
    20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20
    30 permit ip any any

questions.prompt: Which command sequence removes only the entry with sequence number 20 from CLIENTS-IN, leaving entries 10 and 30 in place?
options: R1(config)# no access-list CLIENTS-IN 20
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN, then R1(config-ext-nacl)# delete 20
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN, then R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 20
R1(config)# ip access-list resequence CLIENTS-IN 20 10
questions.explanation: Named ACLs are edited inside their configuration sub-mode, where `no` followed by a sequence number deletes just that entry. Entries 10 and 30 keep their numbers and their counters.

whyWrong.0: `no access-list` takes a number, not a name, and would delete a whole numbered list.
whyWrong.1: There is no `delete` command in ACL configuration mode; an entry is removed with `no` and its sequence number.
whyWrong.3: `resequence` renumbers the entries starting at 20 in steps of 10; it deletes nothing.

questions.prompt: Numbered ACL 101 has five entries and is applied to an interface. To remove one entry the administrator types `no access-list 101 deny tcp any host 10.100.20.30 eq 22` in global configuration mode. What is the result?
options: The entire access list 101 is deleted, not just that entry
Only the matching entry is removed and the others keep their sequence numbers
IOS rejects the command because numbered ACL entries cannot be removed individually
The entry is removed but the ACL is also detached from the interface
questions.explanation: In global configuration `no access-list 101` deletes the whole list regardless of what follows the number, without a warning. The interface keeps its `ip access-group 101` line pointing at a list that no longer exists, so it now permits everything. To delete one entry, open the list with `ip access-list extended 101` and use `no` with the sequence number.

whyWrong.1: That is the behaviour of `no SEQ` inside the named-mode sub-mode, not of the global `no access-list` command.
whyWrong.2: IOS accepts the command — that is the danger.
whyWrong.3: The `ip access-group` line stays on the interface; only the list disappears.

questions.prompt: Which configuration limits SSH and Telnet sessions *to* the router to the source addresses permitted by standard ACL 10?
options: R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 in, on every interface that faces users
R1(config-line)# ip access-group 10 in, under line vty 0 4
R1(config-if)# access-class 10 in, on the management interface
R1(config-line)# access-class 10 in, under line vty 0 4
questions.explanation: `access-class ACL in` is a line-configuration command that filters incoming VTY sessions by source address, whichever interface they arrive on. A standard ACL listing the management hosts is the usual choice.

whyWrong.0: Interface ACLs would work only per interface and would also filter transit traffic.
whyWrong.1: `ip access-group` is not accepted in line configuration mode.
whyWrong.2: `access-class` is a line command, not an interface command.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about how a Cisco router applies IPv4 ACLs to an interface are true? (Choose two.)
options: An outbound ACL filters packets the router itself generates, such as its own pings
An inbound ACL is checked before routing and also filters packets addressed to the router
Two IPv4 ACLs can be applied inbound on the same interface and are evaluated in order
Applying a second ACL in the same direction on an interface replaces the first one
An ACL applied to a LAN interface also filters frames switched between two hosts on that LAN
questions.explanation: Inbound lists run before the routing lookup and see every packet that enters, including SSH or OSPF packets addressed to the router. Only one IPv4 list per direction can be attached; a second `ip access-group … in` silently replaces the first.

whyWrong.0: Outbound ACLs never filter packets the router generates itself, such as its own pings or routing updates.
whyWrong.2: One list per interface, per direction, per protocol — there is no stacking.
whyWrong.4: Traffic between two hosts in the same VLAN never crosses the router, so no router ACL can see it.

exhibit.title: R1# show running-config | section access-list
exhibit.text:
ip access-list extended WEB-ONLY
 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 eq www host 10.100.20.20
 deny ip any any

questions.prompt: WEB-ONLY is applied inbound on the interface facing 10.100.10.0/24. Users on that LAN can no longer open http://10.100.20.20. Why?
options: The deny ip any any must come before the permit for the permit to be evaluated
eq www sits on the source side, so it matches replies from port 80, not requests to it
HTTP must be matched with the number 80; the www keyword is only accepted for UDP
An extended ACL cannot use host for the destination; a wildcard of 0.0.0.0 is required
questions.explanation: A port operator binds to the address that precedes it. Here `eq www` follows the source, so the entry matches only packets with *source* port 80 — the server's replies. A client's request has an ephemeral source port and destination port 80, matches nothing, and hits `deny ip any any`. The operator belongs after `host 10.100.20.20`.

whyWrong.0: Denies placed first would block everything; specific permits go above the deny.
whyWrong.2: IOS accepts both `80` and `www` for TCP and prints `www`.
whyWrong.3: `host` is valid for either address in an extended ACL.

questions.prompt: An administrator enters `access-list 1 permit 10.100.10.0 255.255.255.0`, intending to permit the 10.100.10.0/24 subnet. Which source addresses does the entry actually match?
options: Exactly the 256 addresses in 10.100.10.0/24, because IOS converts a subnet mask to a wildcard
Only the single address 10.100.10.0, because a mask of 255s means an exact match
Any address whose last octet is 0, since the first three octets are ignored
Nothing at all — IOS rejects a wildcard that is not the inverse of a valid mask
questions.explanation: The second value is always read as a wildcard: 255 means ignore, 0 means must match. `255.255.255.0` therefore ignores the first three octets and requires the fourth to be 0, matching addresses like 192.0.2.0 or 10.9.9.0 but not 10.100.10.25. The intended wildcard is `0.0.0.255`.

whyWrong.0: IOS never converts; it stores exactly the wildcard typed.
whyWrong.1: Wildcard 255 bits are *ignored*, the opposite of an exact match.
whyWrong.3: IOS accepts any wildcard pattern, contiguous or not.

questions.prompt: An extended ACL must permit ordinary DNS queries from any client to the server 10.1.1.53 and nothing else. Which entry is correct?
options: permit tcp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 67
permit udp any host 10.1.1.53 eq 53
permit udp any eq 53 host 10.1.1.53
questions.explanation: Client DNS queries travel in UDP datagrams to destination port 53. An ACL entry names one transport protocol, so it must say `udp`, and the `eq 53` after the destination matches the destination port.

whyWrong.0: TCP 53 is used for zone transfers and oversized answers, not for ordinary client queries; a `tcp` entry never matches UDP.
whyWrong.1: Port 67 is the DHCP server port.
whyWrong.3: Placing `eq 53` after the source matches source port 53 — replies from a server, not queries from clients.

cards.front: Numbered ranges for standard IPv4 ACLs?
cards.back: 1–99 and the expanded range 1300–1999.

cards.front: Numbered ranges for extended IPv4 ACLs?
cards.back: 100–199 and the expanded range 2000–2699.

cards.front: The three evaluation rules of every ACL?
cards.back: Top-down; first match wins (nothing below is checked); implicit deny at the end (deny any / deny ip any any, no counter).

cards.front: How do you compute a wildcard mask from a subnet mask?
Meaning of a 0 bit and a 1 bit in a wildcard mask?
cards.back: 0 = the packet's bit must match the address bit; 1 = ignore the bit.

cards.front: Wildcards for /27, /28 and /30?
cards.back: 0.0.0.31, 0.0.0.15, 0.0.0.3 (block size − 1 in the last octet).

cards.front: Block-size shortcut for a wildcard octet?
cards.back: Block size = 256 − mask octet; wildcard octet = block size − 1. Octets to the right are 255, to the left 0.

cards.front: What do `host A.B.C.D` and `any` expand to?
What can a standard ACL match?
cards.back: Only the source IPv4 address — no destination, protocol or port.

cards.front: What can an extended ACL match?
cards.back: Protocol (ip/tcp/udp/icmp/…), source and destination addresses, TCP/UDP ports with eq/neq/lt/gt/range, ICMP types, TCP established.

cards.front: Placement rule: standard vs extended ACL?
cards.back: Standard as close to the destination as possible (it sees only the source); extended as close to the source as possible.

cards.front: Command to apply an ACL to an interface?
cards.back: ip access-group {number | name} {in | out} in interface configuration mode.

cards.front: Command to restrict Telnet/SSH sessions to the router by source address?
cards.back: access-class {number | name} in under line vty 0 4 (usually with a standard ACL).

cards.front: How many IPv4 ACLs can an interface carry?
cards.back: One per direction per protocol: one inbound and one outbound IPv4 list. A second ip access-group in the same direction replaces the first.

cards.front: What does the `established` keyword match?
cards.back: TCP segments with the ACK or RST flag set (everything except the first SYN). Permits return traffic; TCP only; not stateful.

cards.front: Default sequence numbers in a named ACL?
cards.back: First entry 10, then increments of 10 (10, 20, 30…). Entries are evaluated in sequence order, not typing order.

cards.front: Remove only entry 20 from named ACL CLIENTS-IN?
cards.back: ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN, then no 20. Insert above it with 15 permit …

cards.front: Renumber the entries of a named ACL?
cards.back: ip access-list resequence NAME start increment (global), e.g. resequence CLIENTS-IN 100 10 → 100, 110, 120…

cards.front: Effect of `no access-list 101 …` in global config?
cards.back: Deletes the entire numbered list 101, whatever follows the number — no warning. Edit single lines in named mode instead.

cards.front: Two commands to verify an ACL?
cards.back: show access-lists (entries, sequence numbers, match counters); show ip interface (which list is applied inbound/outbound).

cards.front: Does an outbound ACL filter the router's own packets?
cards.back: No — router-generated traffic (its pings, OSPF hellos, syslog) bypasses outbound ACLs. Inbound ACLs do filter packets addressed to the router.

cards.front: What does an applied ACL with no entries (or a misspelt name) do?
cards.back: Permits all traffic — the implicit deny exists only once the list has at least one entry.

tickets.title: Servers reachable, but nobody can SSH to R1 since the new LAN ACL
tickets.scenario: R1 connects the client LAN 10.100.10.0/24 on G0/0 (address 10.100.10.1) to a server LAN on G0/1. This morning a new ACL, CLIENTS-IN, was applied inbound on G0/0 to limit clients to HTTP on WEB (10.100.20.20) and SSH on FILES (10.100.20.30). Both services work. But the help desk can no longer SSH to R1 at 10.100.10.1 from any client, and the SSH attempts simply time out.

exhibits.title: R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
exhibits.text:
Extended IP access list CLIENTS-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq www (231 matches)
    20 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.30 eq 22 (17 matches)
    30 deny ip any any (64 matches)

exhibits.title: R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0 | include access list
exhibits.text:
Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is CLIENTS-IN

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the failed SSH sessions to R1?
options: access-class is missing on the VTY lines, so the router refuses all management sessions
Inbound ACLs also filter packets addressed to the router itself; SSH to 10.100.10.1 matches nothing but entry 30 and is denied
Entry 20 permits SSH only to the file server because eq 22 is on the wrong side of the address
The ACL should be applied outbound; an inbound list cannot see traffic that originates on the LAN
tickets.explanation: An inbound ACL is evaluated for every packet entering the interface, including packets whose destination is the router's own address. An SSH SYN from a client to `10.100.10.1` does not match entry 10 (destination WEB) or entry 20 (destination FILES), so it falls to entry 30 — whose counter of 64 is climbing with every attempt. The servers still work because entries 10 and 20 match them before the deny.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1(config)# ip access-list extended CLIENTS-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 25 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.10.1 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# end
R1# show access-lists CLIENTS-IN
```

tickets.title: The web-only policy is applied, yet clients still reach everything
tickets.scenario: A junior engineer wrote CLIENTS-IN to restrict the 10.100.10.0/24 LAN to HTTP on the web server and applied it inbound on R1's G0/0 an hour ago. Clients can still ping and SSH to every server. The engineer insists the list is applied and shows you the interface output as proof.

exhibits.title: R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0 | include access list
exhibits.text:
Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is CLIENT-IN

exhibits.title: R1# show access-lists
exhibits.text:
Extended IP access list CLIENTS-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.100.20.20 eq www
    20 deny ip 10.100.10.0 0.0.0.255 10.100.20.0 0.0.0.255
    30 permit ip any any

tickets.question: Why is no traffic being filtered?
options: The ACL is applied in the wrong direction for traffic that originates on the LAN
Counters only increment for deny entries, so the ACL is in fact working as designed
The name in ip access-group does not match the list; a list that does not exist permits everything
Named ACLs cannot be used with ip access-group; only numbered lists filter on interfaces
tickets.explanation: The interface references `CLIENT-IN`, but the configured list is `CLIENTS-IN` — names are case-sensitive and must match exactly. IOS accepts a reference to a non-existent list and treats it as empty, and an empty list permits all traffic. The real list shows no match counters at all because nothing has ever been evaluated against it.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group CLIENTS-IN in
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0 | include access list
```

tickets.title: Blocking one PC from the file server took the whole branch offline
tickets.scenario: Branch router R1 has the user LAN 10.100.10.0/24 on G0/0 and the WAN toward head office on G0/1. An administrator was asked to stop PC-B (10.100.10.11) from reaching the head-office file server. Two minutes after the change, every user at the branch lost access to head office and the Internet, and pings to any remote address return an unreachable from 10.100.10.1.

exhibits.title: R1# show access-lists 10
exhibits.text:
Standard IP access list 10
    10 deny   10.100.10.11 (6 matches)

exhibits.title: R1# show ip interface gigabitethernet0/0 | include access list
exhibits.text:
Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is 10

tickets.question: What is the root cause of the outage?
options: The ACL was applied inbound; standard ACLs are only valid outbound on a LAN interface
The list contains only a deny entry, so the implicit deny at the end drops every other host's traffic too
The host entry needs a wildcard mask of 0.0.0.255 before it can match any traffic
A standard ACL cannot deny a single host; an extended ACL with the host keyword is required
tickets.explanation: Every ACL ends with an implicit deny. List 10 explicitly denies PC-B and permits nobody, so every other packet entering G0/0 reaches the end of the list and is dropped — hence the unreachables from R1's own address. A `permit any` is needed after the deny. The placement is also poor: a standard ACL inbound on the LAN blocks PC-B from *everything*, not just the file server; it belongs as close to the destination as possible, or should be an extended ACL naming the server.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit any
R1(config)# end
R1# show access-lists 10
```

questions.prompt: A company wants every host in its branch office to reach headquarters servers across the Internet with encryption, without installing any software on the hosts. Which VPN arrangement fits?
options: A clientless SSL VPN portal on the headquarters ASA
A remote-access IPsec VPN using Secure Client on each host
A site-to-site IPsec VPN between the branch and headquarters routers
A GRE tunnel between the routers with no IPsec applied
questions.explanation: A **site-to-site** VPN terminates on the two gateways. The routers authenticate each other, build IPsec SAs and encrypt everything between the two LANs; the hosts send ordinary packets and never know a VPN exists.

whyWrong.0: A clientless portal serves one user in a browser and reaches only web applications; it does not connect a whole LAN.
whyWrong.1: Remote access puts a client on every device, which is exactly what the requirement rules out.
whyWrong.3: GRE encapsulates and carries multicast, but it provides no encryption at all.

exhibit.title: R1# show crypto ipsec sa | include encaps|decaps|peer|errors
exhibit.text:
current_peer 203.0.113.1 port 500
    #pkts encaps: 1180, #pkts encrypt: 1180, #pkts digest: 1180
    #pkts decaps: 0, #pkts decrypt: 0, #pkts verify: 0
    #send errors 0, #recv errors 0

questions.prompt: R1 terminates a site-to-site IPsec tunnel to R2. Users behind R1 cannot reach servers behind R2. Based on the counters, which statement is most accurate?
options: R1 is encrypting and sending traffic, but nothing is returning — look at R2's side or the return path
R1 never sends anything into the tunnel because its crypto ACL does not match the user traffic
IKE phase 1 has failed on R1, so no IPsec security association exists for this peer
The transform sets differ, so R1 encrypts with a key that R2 is unable to use
questions.explanation: `#pkts encaps` at 1180 proves R1 has a valid SA and is encrypting packets that matched its crypto ACL. `#pkts decaps` at 0 means no ESP has come back: R2's crypto ACL is not the mirror image, R2 has no route to R1's LAN, or something drops protocol 50 toward R1.

whyWrong.1: A non-matching ACL would leave `#pkts encaps` at zero; 1180 packets clearly matched.
whyWrong.2: Packets cannot be encapsulated without an IPsec SA, and an IPsec SA cannot exist without phase 1 succeeding.
whyWrong.3: A transform-set mismatch stops phase 2 from completing, so there would be no SA and no encaps count at all.

questions.prompt: Which two statements about IPsec protocol numbers and ports are correct? (Choose two.)
options: AH is identified by UDP port 51
ESP is IP protocol 50 and has no port number
IKE negotiates security associations over UDP port 500
NAT traversal carries ESP inside TCP port 4500
GRE is IP protocol 50 when it is combined with IPsec
questions.explanation: ESP and AH are Layer 3 protocols identified in the IP header's Protocol field (50 and 51); neither has ports. IKE runs over UDP 500, and NAT-T moves IKE and UDP-wrapped ESP to UDP 4500.

whyWrong.0: AH is IP protocol 51 — a protocol number, not a UDP port.
whyWrong.3: NAT-T uses **UDP** 4500, never TCP.
whyWrong.4: GRE is IP protocol 47 regardless of what protects it; 50 is ESP.

questions.prompt: A teleworker's laptop builds an IKEv2/IPsec tunnel to the corporate ASA from a hotel network that uses PAT. The tunnel comes up and traffic flows normally. Which mechanism makes this possible?
options: The ASA switches the session from IPsec to clientless TLS when it sees a translated source address
IKE falls back to aggressive mode, which does not check the source address of the peer
AH is negotiated instead of ESP, because AH tolerates address changes on the path
NAT-T detects the translation during IKE and wraps each ESP packet in UDP on port 4500
questions.explanation: During IKE both peers exchange hashes of their address and port; a mismatch reveals a NAT. They then move to UDP 4500 and encapsulate ESP in UDP so the PAT device has a port to translate. IKEv2 has this built in.

whyWrong.0: An ASA does not change VPN type mid-session; TLS remote access is a separate configuration and protocol.
whyWrong.1: Aggressive mode only reduces phase 1 to three messages; it does nothing for NAT.
whyWrong.2: AH hashes the IP addresses, so NAT breaks it — the opposite of tolerating address changes.

exhibit.title: Packet captured between the two gateways

questions.prompt: A packet captured on the Internet between two VPN gateways has the structure shown. Which IPsec mode produced it, and how can you tell?
options: Transport mode — the top IP header is the original one and is kept for routing across the Internet
Tunnel mode — a second IP header addressed to the gateways was added in front of the encrypted original
Transport mode — the ESP header sits directly after the first IP header, which is what transport mode does
Tunnel mode — the SPI value in the ESP header is what identifies a GRE tunnel to the receiving gateway
questions.explanation: Only **tunnel mode** adds a new outer IP header. The outer header carries the gateway addresses (`203.0.113.1` and `198.51.100.1`) and the original host-to-host header is inside the encrypted payload — the signature of tunnel mode.

whyWrong.0: In transport mode there is only one IP header, and it carries the real endpoints, not the gateways.
whyWrong.2: ESP follows the IP header in both modes; the presence of a *second*, encrypted IP header is what distinguishes tunnel mode.
whyWrong.3: The SPI identifies the security association, and nothing here indicates GRE — the header after ESP is IP, not GRE.

questions.prompt: Two routers connect their sites with an IPsec crypto map. The administrator wants to run OSPF between the sites so that new subnets are learned automatically. Why is a GRE tunnel added underneath the IPsec protection?
options: GRE compresses OSPF updates so that they fit inside the smaller MTU left after ESP encapsulation
GRE authenticates the OSPF neighbours with its own key, something the IPsec security associations cannot do
GRE carries OSPF's multicast hellos, which ESP alone cannot, and provides a routable tunnel interface
GRE replaces IKE as the key-exchange protocol, so the routers no longer need a matching ISAKMP policy
questions.explanation: A crypto-map IPsec tunnel carries only unicast IP and has no interface, so OSPF's multicast hellos cannot cross it. GRE encapsulates any packet — multicast included — and appears as `Tunnel0`, which OSPF treats as a point-to-point link. IPsec then encrypts the GRE packets.

whyWrong.0: GRE adds 24 bytes of overhead; it compresses nothing.
whyWrong.1: GRE has no authentication; OSPF authentication is configured in OSPF itself.
whyWrong.3: IKE is still required — GRE has no key exchange or encryption of its own.

questions.prompt: Which IPsec service does the Authentication Header (AH) protocol not provide?
options: Confidentiality through encryption of the payload
Integrity through a keyed hash over the packet
Origin authentication of the sending peer
Anti-replay protection using sequence numbers
questions.explanation: AH (IP protocol 51) authenticates and integrity-checks the packet, including fixed IP header fields, and carries a sequence number for anti-replay — but it never encrypts. Confidentiality requires ESP.

whyWrong.1: Integrity is AH's main purpose; its ICV covers the payload and immutable header fields.
whyWrong.2: The keyed hash proves the packet came from a peer holding the key.
whyWrong.3: AH carries a 32-bit sequence number exactly as ESP does.

questions.prompt: Which two statements describe remote-access VPNs correctly? (Choose two.)
options: A client-based remote-access VPN can use TLS with DTLS, or IKEv2/IPsec, as its transport
The hosts on the remote LAN are unaware of the VPN because their gateway handles it for them
The remote user needs a fixed public IP address so that the headend can initiate the tunnel
A clientless VPN gives a browser access to web applications through an HTTPS portal on the headend
Remote-access VPNs authenticate only the two endpoint devices, never the individual user
questions.explanation: Cisco Secure Client connects over TLS (TCP 443) with DTLS (UDP 443) for real-time traffic, or over IKEv2/IPsec. The clientless option needs only a browser and an HTTPS portal on the ASA or FTD, and reaches web-based resources.

whyWrong.1: That describes a site-to-site VPN; in remote access the user's own device runs the client.
whyWrong.2: The client initiates from any address, and NAT-T or TLS handles PAT along the way.
whyWrong.4: Authenticating the individual user through AAA is the defining feature of remote access.

exhibit.text:
IPv4 Crypto ISAKMP SA
dst             src             state          conn-id status
203.0.113.1     198.51.100.1    MM_NO_STATE          0 ACTIVE (deleted)

IPv6 Crypto ISAKMP SA

questions.prompt: A new site-to-site IPsec tunnel between R-BR and R-HQ never passes traffic. What does this output tell you?
options: Phase 1 succeeded and the SA is idle; quick mode is simply waiting for the first interesting packet
Phase 1 failed — the ISAKMP policies or pre-shared keys most likely differ, so no IPsec SA can be built
The peer is reachable and authenticated, but the two crypto ACLs are not mirror images of each other
The tunnel is healthy — MM_NO_STATE is the normal idle state a main-mode SA shows between rekeys
questions.explanation: A healthy phase 1 shows `QM_IDLE`. `MM_NO_STATE` with `(deleted)` means main mode started and collapsed before authentication completed — typically no matching ISAKMP policy, a wrong pre-shared key, or a peer that stopped answering. Without phase 1 there is no phase 2 and no data.

whyWrong.0: An idle, completed phase 1 is `QM_IDLE`, not `MM_NO_STATE`.
whyWrong.2: Mismatched crypto ACLs are a phase 2 problem; phase 1 would still reach `QM_IDLE`.
whyWrong.3: `MM_NO_STATE` is a failure state, and rekeying does not tear the SA down to it.

questions.prompt: In which situation is IPsec transport mode an appropriate choice?
options: Two gateways protecting traffic between the LANs behind them, where the hosts are not IPsec peers
A remote-access user whose real source address must stay hidden from anyone on the Internet path
A site-to-site tunnel that must pass through a NAT device without using NAT traversal
Two routers encrypting a GRE tunnel whose outer header already carries their own addresses
questions.explanation: Transport mode keeps the original IP header, so the IPsec peers must be the packet's real source and destination. A GRE tunnel already has a router-to-router outer header, so ESP in transport mode can protect it and save 20 bytes.

whyWrong.0: When the peers act for other hosts, a new outer header is needed — that is tunnel mode.
whyWrong.1: Hiding the original addresses requires the new outer header of tunnel mode.
whyWrong.2: Neither mode passes ESP through NAT by itself; NAT-T is what solves that.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of IKEv1 phase 1?
options: To create the pair of one-way IPsec security associations that will carry the encrypted user data
To select which packets are interesting by comparing them with the crypto ACL on both peers
To authenticate the peers, run Diffie-Hellman and build one bidirectional ISAKMP SA for further negotiation
To encapsulate the first user packet in ESP and send it so that the peer can learn the SPI
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (main mode, 6 messages, or aggressive mode, 3) agrees an ISAKMP policy, performs a DH exchange and authenticates the peers with a PSK or certificate. Its product is a single bidirectional ISAKMP SA under which phase 2 negotiates the IPsec SAs.

whyWrong.0: The IPsec SA pair is built by phase 2 (quick mode).
whyWrong.1: Interesting traffic is a crypto ACL decision made before IKE is even triggered.
whyWrong.3: ESP carries data only after both phases have completed.

questions.prompt: Why does the tunnel report a transport MTU of 1476 bytes?
options: The 1500-byte physical MTU minus the 20-byte outer IP header and the 4-byte GRE header
The 1500-byte physical MTU minus a 24-byte ESP header added by the IPsec profile
GRE always reserves 24 bytes for its optional key and sequence-number fields
The bandwidth of 100 Kbit/sec limits the tunnel to 1476-byte packets
questions.explanation: Plain GRE over IP adds a new 20-byte IP header and a 4-byte GRE header, 24 bytes in all, so 1500 − 24 = 1476 bytes remain for the original packet.

whyWrong.1: The output says `GRE/IP` with no IPsec; ESP overhead is larger and varies with the cipher.
whyWrong.2: The base GRE header is 4 bytes; the key and sequence fields are optional and shown as disabled here.
whyWrong.3: `BW` is a metric used by routing protocols; it does not constrain packet size.

questions.prompt: A company is adding 40 branch routers to its IPsec design. Which statement correctly compares pre-shared keys with certificates for peer authentication?
options: Pre-shared keys scale better because a single key can be reused on every router without building a PKI
Certificates scale better: each router has its own CA-signed identity, and a compromised device is simply revoked
Certificates remove the need for IKE entirely, because the certificate authority distributes the session keys
Pre-shared keys are stronger than certificates because they never depend on the routers having accurate time
questions.explanation: With certificates nothing secret is shared between peers; each device carries an identity signed by a CA both trust, new sites need no per-peer entry, and a lost router is revoked rather than every key being changed. PSKs are simpler but are per-peer secrets stored in configurations.

whyWrong.0: Reusing one PSK everywhere means one leaked router exposes every tunnel — the opposite of scaling safely.
whyWrong.2: IKE still negotiates and derives the session keys; the CA only vouches for identities.
whyWrong.3: Certificates do need accurate time, but that is an operational requirement, not a weakness in their strength.

questions.prompt: A GRE over IPsec tunnel between R1 and R2 started flapping every minute after OSPF was enabled across it. What is the cause?
options: The IPsec security association lifetime keeps expiring and IKE renegotiates the tunnel each minute
The tunnel MTU is too small for OSPF database description packets, so the adjacency resets
OSPF neighbours are resetting because the tunnel's network type defaults to point-to-point
The WAN subnet is advertised over the tunnel, so R1 routes to its tunnel destination through the tunnel itself
questions.explanation: `%TUN-5-RECURDOWN` means the best route to the tunnel destination now points into the tunnel — recursive routing. It happens when the public WAN subnet is included in the OSPF process: the peer advertises it across the tunnel, R1 installs that specific `/30`, and because a `/30` is a longer prefix than R1's static default route, longest prefix match sends packets for the tunnel destination into the tunnel itself. IOS shuts the tunnel, the route disappears, the tunnel comes back, and the cycle repeats.

whyWrong.0: SA rekeys are seamless and do not log a tunnel-interface state change.
whyWrong.1: An MTU problem would leave the tunnel up while OSPF stuck in EXSTART; it would not log RECURDOWN.
whyWrong.2: Point-to-point is the correct and stable network type for a GRE tunnel.

questions.prompt: Which three components does Cisco DMVPN combine to build a hub-and-spoke overlay with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels?
options: Multipoint GRE, NHRP and IPsec
IPsec VTI, BGP and NAT-T
Clientless TLS, EAP and IKEv2
Point-to-point GRE, static routes and AH
questions.explanation: DMVPN uses a single multipoint GRE interface on the hub, NHRP so spokes register their (possibly dynamic) public addresses and resolve each other, and IPsec to encrypt everything. Spokes then build direct tunnels to each other on demand.

whyWrong.1: VTIs and BGP can be used with DMVPN but are not what defines it; NAT-T is an IKE feature.
whyWrong.2: Those belong to remote-access VPNs, not to a router overlay.
whyWrong.3: Point-to-point GRE and static routes are exactly the scaling problem DMVPN removes, and AH is rarely used.

cards.front: ESP — IP protocol number and services?
cards.back: IP protocol 50. Confidentiality, integrity, origin authentication and anti-replay. No port number.

cards.front: AH — IP protocol number and what it lacks?
cards.back: IP protocol 51. Integrity, authentication, anti-replay — but no encryption. Its hash covers the IP addresses, so NAT breaks it.

cards.front: IKE — transport and port?
cards.back: UDP 500 (IKEv1 in ISAKMP, or IKEv2). Negotiates SAs, authenticates peers, derives keys with Diffie-Hellman.

cards.front: NAT traversal (NAT-T) — port and what it does?
cards.back: UDP 4500. IKE detects a NAT on the path, moves to 4500 and wraps every ESP packet in a UDP header so PAT can track it.

cards.front: GRE — IP protocol number, overhead and default tunnel MTU?
cards.back: IP protocol 47. 24 bytes (20-byte outer IP + 4-byte GRE). Tunnel transport MTU 1476.

cards.front: The four services IPsec provides?
cards.back: Confidentiality (encryption), integrity (keyed hash), origin authentication (only the peer holds the key), anti-replay (sequence numbers).

cards.front: Tunnel mode vs transport mode?
cards.back: Tunnel: new outer IP header (gateway to gateway), whole original packet encrypted. Transport: original IP header kept, only the payload encrypted.

cards.front: When is transport mode used, and what is the IOS default?
cards.back: Host-to-host, or GRE over IPsec (GRE already has the router-to-router header); saves 20 bytes. IOS default is tunnel mode (`mode tunnel`).

cards.front: IKEv1 phase 1 — what does it do, and what does it produce?
cards.back: Matches an ISAKMP policy, runs Diffie-Hellman and authenticates the peers (pre-shared key or certificate). Result: one bidirectional ISAKMP (IKE) SA that protects phase 2.

cards.front: IKEv1 phase 2 — name and result?
cards.back: Quick mode, protected by the phase-1 SA. Agrees the transform set (e.g. ESP with AES and SHA) and installs a pair of one-way IPsec SAs (inbound + outbound) that carry the data.

cards.front: What does IKEv2 add over IKEv1?
cards.back: Fewer messages to build a tunnel, built-in NAT traversal, EAP user authentication, acknowledged messages and anti-DoS cookies. Not backward compatible with IKEv1.

cards.front: What does Diffie-Hellman do in IPsec?
cards.back: Key exchange: both peers compute the same secret from values sent in clear text, so the key itself never crosses the network. IKE runs it in phase 1 (and again in phase 2 with PFS).

cards.front: Encryption and hash algorithms: retired vs recommended?
cards.back: Retired: DES (56-bit), 3DES (168-bit), MD5, SHA-1. Use AES-128/256 (AES-GCM best) with SHA-256 or stronger HMAC.

cards.front: Pre-shared key vs certificates for IKE peer authentication?
cards.back: PSK: same secret on both peers, simple, per-peer, hard to rotate. Certificates: CA-signed identity per device, scale, revocable, need a PKI and accurate time.

cards.front: Site-to-site vs remote-access VPN?
cards.back: Site-to-site: gateway to gateway, hosts need no software, IPsec tunnel mode, always-on. Remote access: one device to a headend, per-user AAA, address from a pool.

cards.front: Client-based vs clientless remote access, and their ports?
cards.back: Client-based: Cisco Secure Client over TLS (TCP 443) + DTLS (UDP 443), or IKEv2/IPsec (UDP 500/4500). Clientless: browser to an HTTPS portal, web apps only.

cards.front: DMVPN components, and what FlexVPN is?
cards.back: DMVPN = multipoint GRE + NHRP + IPsec: hub-and-spoke with dynamic spoke-to-spoke tunnels. FlexVPN = Cisco's IKEv2-only framework on VTIs for any topology.

cards.front: Healthy state in `show crypto isakmp sa`, and what MM_NO_STATE means?
cards.back: `QM_IDLE` = phase 1 complete. `MM_NO_STATE` = main mode failed (policy or key mismatch, peer silent); `MM_KEY_EXCH` = stuck at authentication.

cards.front: In `show crypto ipsec sa`, encaps rising but decaps at 0 means?
cards.back: We encrypt and send; nothing returns. Check the peer's crypto ACL (mirror image), its route to our LAN, and anything dropping IP protocol 50 toward us.

cards.front: Does plain GRE encrypt? Why run GRE over IPsec instead of IPsec alone?
cards.back: GRE encrypts nothing. It carries multicast (so OSPF/EIGRP) and gives a routable tunnel interface; IPsec then encrypts the GRE packets.

tickets.title: Branch lost headquarters after a firewall change — the tunnel says it is up
tickets.scenario: R-BR (`198.51.100.1`) has a site-to-site IPsec tunnel to R-HQ (`203.0.113.1`). Last night the security team replaced the rule set on the Internet firewall in front of R-HQ. This morning nobody at the branch can reach headquarters. The on-call engineer reports that `show crypto isakmp sa` on R-BR "looks fine" and the ISAKMP SA keeps re-establishing without errors.

exhibits.text:

203.0.113.1     198.51.100.1    QM_IDLE           1003 ACTIVE

exhibits.text:
Extended IP access list OUTSIDE-IN
    10 permit udp any host 203.0.113.1 eq isakmp (41 matches)
    20 permit udp any host 203.0.113.1 eq non500-isakmp
    30 permit tcp any host 203.0.113.1 eq 443 (1204 matches)
    40 deny ip any any (2310 matches)

tickets.question: What is the root cause?
options: The pre-shared key on R-HQ was changed during the maintenance, so authentication fails on every attempt
The firewall permits IKE (UDP 500) and NAT-T (UDP 4500) but drops ESP, IP protocol 50, so R-BR's encrypted packets never reach R-HQ
R-BR's crypto ACL no longer matches the branch subnet, so user traffic leaves in the clear and is dropped at HQ
The IPsec SA lifetime expired and the tunnel is stuck renegotiating phase 2 with the peer
tickets.explanation: Phase 1 is healthy (`QM_IDLE`) because IKE on UDP 500 is permitted — line 10 has matches. Phase 2 also negotiates over IKE, so R-BR installs an IPsec SA and encrypts: `#pkts encaps` is 2310. But ESP is IP protocol 50, not a UDP port, and nothing in `OUTSIDE-IN` permits it; the `deny ip any any` counter shows exactly 2310 drops. R-HQ never receives a single ESP packet, so it never replies and `#pkts decaps` stays at 0.
tickets.fix:
```ios
HQ-FW(config)# ip access-list extended OUTSIDE-IN
HQ-FW(config-ext-nacl)# 25 permit esp any host 203.0.113.1
HQ-FW(config-ext-nacl)# end
```
After the change, `#pkts decaps` on R-BR starts climbing and the deny counter stops. A VPN gateway behind a firewall needs UDP 500, UDP 4500 **and** IP protocol 50.

tickets.question: Why does the tunnel never establish?
options: The crypto ACLs on the two routers are not mirror images, so quick mode rejects the proxy identities
The pre-shared keys differ, so the peers fail authentication in the last two main-mode messages
No ISAKMP policy matches: R-BR proposes AES-256, SHA-256 and DH group 14, while R-HQ only accepts AES-128, SHA-1 and group 2
R-HQ has no route back to 198.51.100.1, so its main-mode replies never leave the router
tickets.explanation: Phase 1 only succeeds if both peers have a policy whose encryption, hash, authentication method and DH group all match. R-BR offers AES-256 / SHA-256 / PSK / group 14; R-HQ's only policy is AES-128 / SHA-1 / PSK / group 2. R-HQ answers "no proposal chosen", the SA is deleted at `MM_NO_STATE`, and phase 2 never starts — hence no IPsec SAs. A key mismatch would get further, to `MM_KEY_EXCH`, because DH completes before authentication.
tickets.fix:
```ios
R-HQ(config)# crypto isakmp policy 10
R-HQ(config-isakmp)# encryption aes 256
R-HQ(config-isakmp)# hash sha256
R-HQ(config-isakmp)# group 14
R-HQ(config-isakmp)# end
R-HQ# clear crypto isakmp
```
Alternatively add a second, lower-numbered policy on R-HQ with the stronger settings. After the change, `show crypto isakmp sa` on both routers shows `QM_IDLE` and the IPsec SA pair appears.
